articles.title: Tor hit by major DDoS attack, forced to release emergency update to users
articles.content: The Tor Project releases urgent updates after large-scale DDoS attacks overwhelmed relay operators across the network Attackers flooded relays with circuit requests, causing resource exhaustion, degraded performance, and lost relay functionality Maintainers say the attacks are ongoing and adaptive, urging operators to upgrade immediately and watch for further fixes The Tor Project seems to be experiencing major Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks which have gotten so disruptive that they forced the release of an update in order to address it. Now, Tor Project says “most relay operators” were affected by an ongoing DDoS attack. “This release comes in rapid response to the ongoing DDoS attack on the network, which has affected most relay operators,” the patch notes read. “This is not an easy problem to address, as relays across the network are being overwhelmed by a massive flood of client circuits. We are actively evaluating additional defenses and so expect further releases in the near future.” Second patch Tor is a privacy-focused network that routes internet traffic through multiple relays (servers operated by volunteers), allowing users to hide their identities and online activities. The relays work by receiving and forwarding encrypted traffic between users and other parts of the network, and are divided into three categories: Guard (or entry) relays (the first point of contact between a Tor user and the network), Middle relays (these pass traffic between them and add layers of separation), and Exit relays (these send traffic from the Tor network back to the regular internet and the user’s final destination). The patch brings Tor to version 0.4.9.17 and includes a series of security fixes, including, according to the patch notes, one “especially important for relay DoS defenses related to IPv6 handling." The project now urges relay operators to upgrade to the latest version as soon as possible, and to keep an eye out for additional updates. It did not share any details about the ongoing DDoS attack. This doesn’t seem to be the first patch the Tor Project released in response to the DDoS attacks, either. Approximately three weeks ago, Tor version 0.4.9.15 was introduced, also in response to attacks. This version, however, seems not to have worked properly. “Tor relay operators are reporting renewed denial-of-service (DoS) attacks despite security mitigations introduced in Tor 0.4.9.15 on October 28,” a Reddit user said in a thread on “renewed DoS attacks”.. “On November 9, one operator reported that two relays lost their HSDir flags after attacks caused severe CPU and memory exhaustion. Another operator reported similar activity on November 10, including thousands of circuit creation requests per second.” The operator said the reports suggest whoever is behind these attacks managed to bypass Tor’s recent protections. “The full scope of the attacks and their impact on the wider Tor network are not clear,” they said. Reddit activity Reddit has quite a few threads from different Tor users complaining about nodes being saturated and the network being slow or outright unresponsive. On November 9, a person on the Tor Project’s forum said the attacker “successfully stripped the HSDir flag from two [of their] relays” in a few hours, and that one attack saw “high asymmetric egress and one saw high asymmetric ingress (although not nearly as much as the old attacks).” Both relays lost their HSDir flags as a result. At press time, no threat actors claimed responsibility for the attacks, so we don’t know who they are or what their motives are. What we do know is that the attacks appear persistent and adaptive, and that relay operators reported multiple waves of attacks and changes in attack patterns. Whether or not the latest patch finally addresses the attacks in full, remains to be seen. The project maintainers seem to be confident about it. “Thank you to all… except our attacker(s),” they said in conclusion. Via…

articles.title: Jensen Huang's Fall Hits 'Open' Models In Boost to Anthropic and OpenAI
articles.content: Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia could weaken the open AI model ecosystem he spent years championing, potentially strengthening closed-model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic, according to the Financial Times. From the report: The US chip giant's former chief threw Nvidia's balance sheet into creating a broad AI ecosystem, including by seeding and acquiring start-ups involved in the development of open-source and open-weight models, which users can customize and run on their own hardware. Huang was a forceful advocate for their spread, lobbying against Washington's moves to restrict the use of Chinese-made open models while seeking the development of US alternatives. "Our AI leadership will be judged not by one frontier AI model, but by whether the United States builds a strong, open ecosystem that diffuses into every sector," he wrote this summer in his first-ever message on X. His ignominious exit from Nvidia deprives the open model sector of its most vocal and influential supporter in the US. "I think Jensen stood to gain the most economically and was personally committed to diversity at the model layer," said one venture capitalist who has invested in AI start-ups alongside Nvidia. "Without him and a less generous Nvidia in terms of investment, we may end up in a much more concentrated world of model providers." Whether Nvidia will continue the rapid pace of dealmaking under a new leader is unclear. The company was expected to participate in or lead four start-up deals currently under discussion: investments in Thinking Machines Lab and Groq, a potential partnership with Reflection AI and the $12.9bn acquisition of open model repository Hugging Face. "Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," said Elon Musk in a post on X on Saturday. "Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost." "In some sense [Huang leaving Nvidia] is bad for the industry, but in some sense Jensen is an enemy of the frontier labs because he wants models to become commoditized so he retains the prime position in the value chain," said one senior figure at a leading Silicon Valley AI company. "I don't think open weight models are going away... but losing Jensen as their greatest financial backer and champion will slow their progress, and I imagine will not hurt Anthropic's IPO," said another industry figure. "It's reasonable to expect the ouster of Jensen will concentrate computing power more in the hands of frontier labs and hyperscalers," added a senior figure at an AI lab. "That's good for the labs." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: MongoDB snaps up Firebolt to bring transactions and analytics under one roof
articles.content: MongoDB has acquired analytical database specialist Firebolt in another attempt to bring transactional and analytical workloads onto one platform. The document database vendor carved out its patch of the database market with flexible, JSON-like documents rather than rigid, predefined table structures. Developers put it to work in web, mobile, ecommerce, and content management applications. It has since branched out to offer a data platform it says is ready for the age of AI and AI agents working across transactional environments, promising scale, speed and reliability. Firebolt was founded in Israel in 2019. It built a cloud-native data warehouse based on the notion of automatically and transparently merging and compacting files as they are ingested. Speaking to The Register in 2020 , then CTO Eldad Farkash claimed this slashes the amount of data users need to load into the system, accelerating query performance and improving concurrency. Firebolt raised $100 million in Series C funding in 2022 at a reported valuation of $1.4 billion. MongoDB has not disclosed the acquisition price. But what will it get, and what does that mean for MongoDB users? In a blog post , the company said: "By integrating Firebolt into MongoDB's Intelligent Data Platform, we're bringing a high-performance analytics engine to where your operational data already lives. Firebolt's engine will run right alongside your database, and we'll keep it in sync automatically, so there's no pipeline to build or manage. You'll get one platform for operational and real-time analytical workloads, so teams can ship faster, with fewer systems to operate and secure." The integration isn't available yet. MongoDB says customers will gain access in the coming months, while existing Firebolt customers will retain their current service and support. MongoDB's pitch is that AI agents will need fresh operational data and fast analytical answers, without customers having to stitch separate platforms together. MongoDB is hardly the first vendor to chase that combination. Bringing online transaction processing (OLTP) and online analytical processing (OLAP) together promises less infrastructure to manage and fewer data pipelines to maintain. Delivering both without compromises is the harder part. Earlier this year, Databricks claimed to have cracked the problem , promising "one data, zero compromises, zero copies." It works with Reyden – a new compute engine – and Lakebase, its serverless PostgreSQL on open object storage. Rivals pointed out there were briefly two copies of the data in the system at some level. SingleStore also tackles the problem with an in-memory row store and an on-disk column store with tiered storage, "meaning transactions hit memory first, and then they roll off to disk storage," allowing analytics and transactions on a single system. Oracle and SAP have also spent years adding analytical capabilities to transactional platforms to reduce the delay between recording data and analyzing it. MongoDB promises real-time analytics without a customer-managed pipeline. Whether that also means avoiding separate copies of the data is less clear. Automatic synchronization doesn't explain how the information is stored or moved underneath. The Register has asked MongoDB to clarify the architecture. MongoDB has been here before. In 2022, it unveiled columnstore indexing designed to help developers build analytical queries into their applications. The idea was to accelerate those queries without changing the document structure or moving data to another system. Firebolt gives MongoDB another tool for a familiar job: making analytics feel at home beside its operational database. Whether the plumbing lives up to the pitch remains to be seen. ®

articles.title: What to watch tonight: 61 new shows and movies just added to Netflix, Prime Video and more — including a charming Christmas film starring Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki (Nov. 18)

articles.title: Vulcan failure caused by inadequate fuel supply to engines, ULA says
articles.content: United Launch Alliance said Wednesday that the failure of its Vulcan rocket during a launch on Sunday was caused by inadequate fuel supply. "ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday," the company said in a statement . "While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines." The new information released by ULA confirms reporting from Ars Technica on Tuesday that the rocket's failure was not due to the performance of the vehicle's main engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. articles.title: ‘Absurd ambition’: Pulumi expands into software delivery with AI agents that ship and fix code
articles.content: Pulumi CEO Joe Duffy says AI is allowing the company to build products it had aspired to get to for years. (Pulumi Photo) Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on. The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks. “The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy , the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.” The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient. Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime. Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript. The new products take that approach further: Pulumi Delivery lets engineers and AI agents write the steps for releasing software, from testing to sign-off to rollout, as code. An AI reviewer can judge how risky each change is and either send it live or hand it to a person. Pulumi Agents are AI agents for jobs such as investigating outages, cutting cloud costs and fixing security problems. Each one has limits on what it can touch, and every change it makes shows up as proposed code the team can review. To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops. Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide. “Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.” Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans. Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code. “I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said. AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own. Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through…

articles.title: How Orkes ParticleDB turns an impressive demo into a remarkable application
articles.content: Building an AI agent that performs an impressive demonstration is one thing. Building one that can reliably process financial transactions, handle customer refunds, or make business decisions without compromising sensitive data is quite another. That distinction is becoming increasingly important as enterprises move from experimenting with generative AI to deploying agentic applications in production. Developers need more than powerful language models. They need dependable access to enterprise data, orchestration, security, fault tolerance, and a way to explain what an AI agent actually did. Orkes believes its newly previewed ParticleDB can help solve a significant part of that problem. In an interview last month with The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi at AgentCon and MCPCon 2026 in San Jose, California, Orkes co-founder and CEO Jeu George discussed how the company’s emerging database technology and established Conductor orchestration platform are designed to make enterprise AI development simpler and more dependable. Why ParticleDB matters to developers At its recent Orkes Shift developer conference in San Francisco, the company previewed ParticleDB , an agentic database designed to bring together data capabilities that conventionally require multiple systems. Enterprise developers frequently work with relational databases, key-value stores, vector databases, and analytical systems. Connecting these technologies often means building complex extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, managing data movement, and maintaining infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to operate. ParticleDB’s premise is that these capabilities should work together within a common engine, reducing the integration burden on development teams. George contends that the need becomes especially pressing when AI agents enter the picture. “When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data.” —Orkes CEO Jeu George “When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data,” George told The New Stack . That data, however, often resides within tightly controlled enterprise environments. Companies cannot simply expose sensitive customer information, financial records, or proprietary business processes to autonomous agents. George envisions a different approach: Rather than allowing agents to roam freely through enterprise systems, a trusted platform supplies the specific information and context they need. Combined with Orkes Conductor, ParticleDB is intended to keep applications, agents and their underlying data closely integrated within customers’ cloud boundaries. Reliability is still the hardest problem Beyond data integration, George emphasized a familiar challenge for distributed-systems developers: Things inevitably break. Network outages, software bugs, infrastructure failures, and security incidents are unavoidable. With AI agents potentially executing workflows for hours or even days, recovering from failure without duplicating transactions becomes essential. “If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application.” “If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application,” George said. Orkes Conductor addresses that problem through workflow orchestration, recovery mechanisms, security controls, and audit trails. Developers can combine deterministic business processes with AI-driven decisions while retaining visibility into individual actions. For regulated industries such as banking and insurance, that visibility is particularly valuable. Organizations need to reconstruct an agent’s decisions, identify which models and systems were involved, and explain outcomes to customers or regulators. Knowing when…

articles.title: Crypto Market Cycles: Reading the Phases Before You Buy
articles.content: Why do investors become eager to buy assets that attracted little interest before? The change often has as much to do with confidence as with the asset itself. You see that in bonds and shares, and in the enthusiasm and anxiety surrounding crypto. When learning how to buy crypto , earlier cycles can help you judge those shifts and possible entry opportunities, even though they won't tell you exactly where prices go next. Read the shift in buying and selling Economic conditions and investors' changing expectations influence how much buying or selling pressure a market faces. Crypto can move through sharp changes quickly, though its cycles have no fixed duration. When buyers become less willing to meet sellers' prices, downward pressure can build. Interest may eventually return, beginning another advance. The familiar cycle model groups this behaviour into accumulation, markup, distribution and markdown. Their boundaries are often clearer afterwards than while you are deciding what to do. Accumulation after a sell-off A severe sell-off leaves plenty of investors discouraged. Some give up their holdings, trading becomes quieter and prices may settle into a range well below the earlier highs. This is the setting described as accumulation. You can see that the market has fallen; you cannot yet know whether it has finished falling. Patient value investors, including some large holders or whales, consider the depressed price worth accepting the risk. They build a position in anticipation of renewed interest. Markup brings the buyers back As successive peaks exceed previous highs and pullbacks stop above earlier lows, the advance becomes easier to follow. This is the bull market described by the markup stage. Technically minded investors track the pattern, while media attention draws more people towards crypto. A temporary fall now looks to many buyers like a chance to enter the rising market. More newcomers bring more trading, and the rise can continue even as prices become hard to justify on the asset's merits. Buyers start depending on someone else paying a higher price, which is the greater-fool argument rather than a judgement of value. As the advance loses momentum, people who hesitated earlier can rush in together, treating it as their chance to join the rally. That late burst of buying can send prices sharply higher. Distribution divides buyers and holders After an extended rise, prices may stop making progress. Buyers expecting further gains meet holders who see little upside left and want to realise profits. Trading can stay busy while prices fluctuate inside a range. Optimists regard the pause as preparation for another climb; pessimists see the advance running out of strength. With neither view settled, the confidence of the rising market gives way to uncertainty. Markdown puts exits under pressure Markdown is the point at which the excitement of the rally turns into anxiety. To find a buyer, sellers may have to accept progressively lower prices, taking the market back towards levels it passed on the way up. People still buy, but demand at the earlier prices has weakened. Investors concerned with cutting losses can keep selling despite encouraging news, so good headlines alone may not stop the decline. Selling after the decline has begun can mean accepting less profit than you had expected, or a larger loss on an already losing position. Holding leaves your return exposed to any further fall, although a recovery is also possible. Why analysts disagree about the next cycle An accumulation label often comes with a bullish longer-term forecast; a distribution label can signal that an analyst expects weakness. Some forecasts also lean on the Bitcoin halving . This scheduled cut halves miners' subsidy of newly issued bitcoin once per 210,000 blocks, approximately every four years. Earlier rallies have encouraged comparisons with that rhythm, but a reduction in new issuance cannot guarantee the demand needed to sustain another…

articles.title: Google Pixel bug is making lock screen transition animations disappear
articles.content: Credit: Joe Maring / Android Authority TL;DR Pixel owners are reporting an issue with the lock screen animation. Instead of fading to black after pressing the power button, the screen immediately turns off. Users are blaming the November update for the missing animation. Pixel phones have been dealing with some animation problems as of late. Yesterday, we reported on an animation bug causing visual ghosting when closing an app via the recent apps screen. Now, users are running into a problem with the lock screen animation. When you lock your Pixel phone, you’ll normally see a subtle animation before the screen turns off. This animation is a fading effect, which sees the screen gradually transition to black. When waking the phone, the same fading effect is used. It serves as a more visually pleasant way to turn your screen off and on than having the screen immediately go dark or turn on.

articles.title: Meet Superplane: HackerNoon Company of the Week
articles.content: Hey Hackers, Welcome to another HackerNoon Company of the Week feature. Every week, we highlight a standout company from our Tech Company Database that's making waves in the global tech ecosystem and the lives of its users. Our database features everything from S&P giants to rising stars in the Startup scene. This week, we’re excited to spotlight on Superplane , an open-source AI software factory and DevOps control plane designed to automate routine engineering and workflow tasks. Want to be featured on HackerNoon’s Company of the Week? Join HackerNoon's Business Blogging Program! Get to Know SuperPlane SuperPlane is an open-source AI orchestration platform designed to automate routine software development tasks while keeping engineers in control. Rather than requiring developers to manage AI coding agents individually, SuperPlane brings them together in a structured workflow that takes tasks from the backlog to verified, review-ready pull requests. The platform works by analyzing a team's codebase and backlog to identify tasks suitable for automation. Once a task is selected, SuperPlane coordinates AI agents through planning, coding, testing, and review, applying consistent rules and quality checks throughout the process. If something goes wrong, the system provides feedback and prompts the agent to try again, involving a human engineer when additional judgment is needed. SuperPlane integrates with existing development tools, allowing teams to choose their preferred AI models and deploy the platform in the cloud or on-premises. The company reports that its approach can autonomously handle 30% of backlog issues, reduce engineer involvement in routine tasks by 70%, and accelerate the process from issue to reviewed pull request by four times. Founded by Darko Fabijan and Marko Anastasov, the team behind the continuous integration platform Semaphore, SuperPlane aims to reduce repetitive engineering work so developers can focus on more complex problems and higher-value projects. For SuperPlane, the business blogging program offered an opportunity to bring their best foot forward, and truly demonstrate their technical prowess to a relevant audience. articles.title: Apple outranks Walmart and Amazon on efforts to curb toxic chemicals in products and packaging
articles.content: Most companies are backsliding when it comes to consumer safety, but Apple bucked the trend in a new review that found nearly half of the retailers reassessed lost ground on toxic chemicals and plastics. Image credit: Apple Apple earned the highest score and the only A in Toxic-Free Future's 2026 Retailer Report Card. The average grade across 50 major retailers in the United States and Canada remained a D+. IKEA, Target, and Sephora followed Apple with A- grades. The report evaluates how retailers disclose and address hazardous chemicals and plastics in their products, packaging, and supply chains. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: The beginning of a beautiful friendship? Interaction could be key to human acceptance of robots
articles.content: Whether people accept humanoid robots depends not only on what the robots can do for us, but above all on how we experience interacting with them—through all our senses and over time. This is the conclusion of a research team at the University of Potsdam that examined the psychological foundations of humanoid robot acceptance. Technical performance, safety, and the ability to meet human needs are not the only factors that determine acceptance. Instead, acceptance emerges from a dynamic interplay of perception and social interaction, as humans and robots respond to and influence each other.

articles.title: Architecture Decisions Are Bets: A Senior Engineer’s Playbook for Choosing the Right Trade-offs
articles.content: One framework, six real-world dilemmas, and the hidden costs most teams miss Every architecture decision is a bet. You are betting that your traffic will grow a certain way. That your team will stay a certain size. That a vendor will still exist in three years. That the “temporary” fix will actually be temporary. Junior engineers look for the right answer. Senior engineers know there usually isn’t one. There is only the best bet for this team, with these constraints, at this moment — and a plan for what to do if the bet goes wrong. In this post, I’ll share the framework I use to make those bets, walk through six dilemmas that show up in almost every growing system, and point out the second-order costs that usually get ignored until production finds them for you. Step 0: Frame the Problem Before You Touch the Whiteboard Most bad architecture isn’t caused by picking the wrong technology. It’s caused by solving the wrong problem. Before I compare options, I answer five questions: What problem are we actually solving? When someone says “we need microservices,” I keep asking why until I hit the real driver. It’s usually one of three things: deploy speed, team autonomy, or scaling one specific hot path. Each of those has a different (and often cheaper) solution. What are the hard constraints? Latency budget, peak throughput, budget, compliance (GDPR, HIPAA, PCI), and — the one everybody forgets — the skills of the team that will be on call for this at 3 a.m. What are the quality attributes, ranked? You can’t maximize availability, consistency, cost, and simplicity all at once. Force a ranking. “Correctness over latency” is a decision; “everything matters” is not. What does success look like in numbers? “Fast” is not a requirement. “p99 under 200 ms at 5,000 requests per second” is. Who else is affected? Product, ops, security, finance. They surface constraints you’d never find in the code. Then I write it all on one page. If I can’t explain the problem and constraints on a single page, I don’t understand it well enough to design for it. The Framework: Reversibility × Blast Radius Not every decision deserves the same amount of debate. The most useful filter I know is to score each decision on two axes: Reversibility: How expensive is it to undo this in a year? Swapping a logging library is cheap. Migrating your primary database is a multi-quarter project. Blast radius: If we’re wrong, how much breaks? One service, or the whole company? This gives you four zones: Easy to reverse, small blast radius → Just decide. Let the team that owns it pick, and move on. Debating these is the most common waste of senior engineering time. Easy to reverse, large blast radius → Experiment. Use feature flags, canaries, and gradual rollouts. Let data decide. Hard to reverse, small blast radius → Contain it. Put it behind an interface so that if it’s wrong, the damage stays local. Hard to reverse, large blast radius → Slow down. Prototype, write an ADR, get reviews. This is where your seniority actually earns its keep. Amazon calls this one-way vs. two-way doors. The key insight is that a lot of seemingly one-way decisions can be turned into two-way decisions with a bit of upfront design — an abstraction layer, a migration path, a vendor-neutral API. Making decisions reversible is often more valuable than making them correct. Now let’s put the framework to work. Dilemma 1: Synchronous APIs vs. Event-Driven Communication The scenario: You run an online store. When a payment succeeds, the order service must start fulfillment and the inventory service must deduct stock. Flash sales push traffic 20× above normal. Option A: The payment service calls the order and inventory services directly over REST. Option B: The payment service publishes a PaymentConfirmed event to Kafka, and downstream services consume it independently. With synchronous calls, the payment service’s latency becomes the sum of its dependencies, and its availability becomes the product of…

articles.title: The Hidden TCO Trap of Cryptographic Capability Attenuation via Ephemeral Token Proof-of-Possession…
articles.content: The Hidden TCO Trap of Cryptographic Capability Attenuation via Ephemeral Token Proof-of-Possession (AI Governance fiduciary liability): Beyond Token Pricing Why infrastructure overhead, cold starts, and evaluations dwarf raw model API costs Visualizing the hidden architectural and compute overhead of cryptographic capability attenuation in autonomous systems. 📊 Executive Summary: While executives obsess over LLM API token costs, the true margin killer in regulated agentic AI is cryptographic authorization overhead. Implementing ephemeral Proof-of-Possession and capability attenuation to satisfy fiduciary AI governance introduces severe cold-start latencies that effortlessly dwarf raw inference costs, demanding a fundamental infrastructure re-architecture. The Latency Death Spiral: When Autonomous Agents Meet Fiduciary Proof-of-Possession At precisely 09:00 UTC on a Tuesday, a Tier-1 global bank initiated the production deployment of a sovereign, multi-hop agentic workflow engineered to automate cross-border commercial loan origination. The core Large Language Model (LLM) API was flawlessly optimized, processing high-complexity credit analyses at a raw inference cost of roughly $0.04 per transaction. Yet, within twenty minutes of ingesting live traffic, the deployment triggered a cascading latency death spiral that shattered the designated service-level agreements. The failure had nothing to do with the neural network’s prompt processing or output generation. Instead, the architecture collapsed under its own security weight because every autonomous sub-agent in the workflow was strictly mandated to mint, attest, and verify ephemeral Proof-of-Possession (PoP) keys for every outbound request to satisfy boardroom-mandated zero-trust boundaries (Fett et al., 2023; Prakash, 2026). In an attempt to comply with RFC 9449 standardizing Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession (DPoP), the orchestration layer required each agent hop to negotiate asymmetric cryptographic signatures in real-time, effectively paralyzing the data pipeline. The financial post-mortem of this deployment revealed a devastating unit economic reality that offshore IT integrators fundamentally missed during sandbox testing. The actual cost of operating the autonomous workflow was not the heavily negotiated LLM token pricing, but rather the crushing infrastructure overhead of the authorization mechanism itself. As leading identity providers noted in late 2026, forcing high-throughput resource APIs to execute per-request asymmetric cryptographic verification for DPoP introduces massive compute overhead at the API Gateway layer (Fett et al., 2023). Because the bank’s legacy deployment relied on serverless cloud functions to evaluate these cryptographic capabilities on-the-fly, every discrete API call suffered severe cold starts and key generation cycles. This execution penalty spiked the compute Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) from the anticipated $0.04 to an unsustainable $1.20 per transaction. The gross margin of the enterprise AI product was entirely obliterated by the overhead of mathematically proving that the agent actually possessed the authority to execute its delegated tasks. Fresh empirical telemetry from production incident analyses highlights the exact dimensions of this architectural bottleneck. Standard cold-path validation latencies for asymmetric DPoP signatures routinely hit 32.7ms per evaluation in serverless environments. In a basic conversational chat interface, a 30-millisecond delay is imperceptible to a human user. However, in an autonomous multi-hop agent chain executing 50 sequential steps to compile a syndicated loan packet, that delay compounds aggressively. The agent spends more time waiting for the infrastructure to decrypt, validate, and evaluate its cryptographic payload than it spends generating intelligence. This transforms the promise of agentic velocity into an insurmountable financial and operational trap. Datalog Cold Starts and the Math of…

articles.title: Building Self-Maintaining API Documentation with AI Agents
articles.content: If you have ever opened a pull request from a coding agent like Cursor, scrolled through a long diff and found that the only real change was one reworded sentence, you already know where this story starts. I keep our API reference in sync with a live stage OpenAPI file. The staging environment moves fast, and the docs have to follow it before developers and their coding agents copy the old version into real client code. If you are looking to learn more about api doc automations and agentic workflows, check out my book here : The AI Native Technical Writer The above plan looks fine on paper, but it starts to fall apart once it runs against a real stage environment, and it fails in four specific ways. Wording changes became work: Someone rewrote a description on stage. Nothing about the contract changed, but I still got a pull request to review. Unrelated changes piled up: Three products changed on the same day and landed in one giant review that nobody wanted to own. The same change got drafted twice: An open draft already covered Monday’s change, and Thursday’s run drafted it again. A broken deploy looked like a real change: A bad deploy dropped a big chunk of routes for a while, and the model was ready to document that the API had vanished. All four problems had the same cause. I was asking an AI to answer questions that plain code answers better, so I changed the order of the system. Now a regular Node.js watcher does the hard work. The AI only drafts after the change is already classified, and a person still merges every pull request. This post walks through this design. It works for OpenAPI, but the same idea fits protobuf, GraphQL or any contract that moves faster than the people who keep its consumers up to date. The real problem is contract drift “The docs are out of date” sounds like a writing problem, but what actually goes wrong is API contract drift. The staging environment says one thing, the written contract says another and developers trust the written one, so coding agents trust it too. When the two disagree, people ship client code against a shape the API no longer has. The usual fixes don’t help much. Waiting for someone to mention the change in Slack is too slow. Regenerating Markdown from the whole OpenAPI spec every night is too much work, because every run produces a huge diff and reviewers stop reading carefully. Before a model writes a single sentence, I want answers to five questions: Did the contract change, or only the wording? Which product area owns this change? Is this a new endpoint, or a change to an existing one? Did we already draft this in an open pull request? Is stage healthy, or did a broken deploy just delete a lot of routes? Each of these has a correct answer that code can compute. A model should never be guessing them. How the pieces fit together The system has two parts, and each one has a single job. The watcher is a scheduled GitHub Action that runs Node.js. It notices changes, classifies them, splits them into groups and refuses to act when the stage looks broken. The drafting agent is a Cursor Automation with strict rules. It takes one group of changes and turns it into one draft docs pull request. Step 1: Store the API one endpoint at a time The watcher never compares yesterday’s full JSON file with today’s as one big file. It starts by fetching the stage spec: node watch.mjs fetch --out /tmp/stage-doc.json Then it splits the spec into one small snapshot file per operation. An operation is one method and path pair, like these: POST /api/v1/sessions GET /api/v1/sessions/{id} POST /api/v1/billing/invoices ... Each snapshot holds the operation and the schemas it needs, so it can be read and compared on its own. This looks like extra bookkeeping at first, but it changes how every later step behaves: Small diffs. A change to one endpoint no longer creates a 5,000-line pull request. A local baseline. The snapshot files travel with each pull request, so merging one updates the baseline…

articles.title: Waymo has stopped its robotaxis from driving on the freeway—here’s why
articles.content: Waymo is currently restricting its fleet of robotaxis to surface streets after getting into hot water with California over its cars' driving behavior on highways. Specifically, the software tends to drive into construction zones at speed. As first reported by the San Francisco Business Times , this behavior actually drew the ire of California’s DMV earlier this month, which ordered Waymo to stop driving on Californian highways immediately and until it can convince the DMV that its cars no longer “pose an imminent hazard to public safety.” This is not Waymo’s first run-in with this problem. In Arizona, Waymo robotaxis did not recognize ramp closure signs on six occasions in Phoenix in April and entered construction zones. A month later in California, seven Waymo robotaxis entered lanes with active construction. In June, Waymo recalled the almost 3,800 robotaxis capable of highway driving. That problem led Waymo to stick to surface streets only in California after the May incidents until late July, when the robotaxis resumed highway operations. In early July, Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration that it began updating the robotaxi software to a version that “improve[s] the recognition of freeway construction zones, more appropriately prioritize[s] construction zones over other freeway hazards, and reduce[s] speed when the AV detects that it may be in a construction zone.” Read full article Comments

articles.title: The wrong setting for AI cache can cost you a lot of cash
articles.content: Be wary of AI costs. You may be spending more than you think and end up with nothing to show for it but an eye-popping invoice. Register readers are finding themselves on the sharp, pointy end of AI billing, confused about which costs are covered by what, and surprised by "features" that burn through credit, seemingly without warning. Startups without the deep pockets of established companies are the first to feel the squeeze. Sometimes, the approach feels more like an app that urges users to deposit extra cash to keep that streak going than a helpful coding assistant. Take one reader, who told The Register about Claude burning through credits at a ferocious rate after a cache setting was reset in the background. The cache setting controlled how long Claude "remembered" requests and was set to one hour. It's a useful feature, and it lets Claude reuse material that has already been processed. Once it expires, continuing unfinished work can mean paying to process old material again. "After hitting my $200 Ultra plan limit," our reader told us, "I bought $250 in additional credits to finish 8 coding threads." There didn't seem to be much work left to do, so the extra credits should have been plenty. Alas, no, after just under two hours, the entire balance was gone, and no meaningful progress was made. They dug deeper and found that the newer request had switched back to the five-minute cache "without my action or knowledge." The figures didn't add up either, so he made a request to Anthropic to explain the cache setting change and the cost discrepancy. "I found myself stuck with its support chatbot, Fin. It described the cache switch behavior as a 'feature' and said it couldn't provide the reconciliation or investigation." The support thread was then closed. Our reader asked again for an explanation. "Fin kept closing the support thread, sometimes just 31 seconds after I asked for human escalation." The Register asked Anthropic for an explanation, and how users might reach a human when a chatbot comes to the end of its usefulness, but the company has yet to respond. It's all a bit of a cautionary tale. Our reader said, "The money was gone, the work was unfinished, and I was spending time chasing answers that I needed to spend building my app. "I wish I'd known this could happen before buying those credits." Indeed. There are endless stories of how using AI has resulted in unexpected costs. Even celebrity mathematician Dr Hannah Fry found the token costs of sending an agent on an errand a surprise. And then there are the misunderstandings when credits gifted under one program turn out to be inapplicable for another, and support teams play a variant of ping-pong , just with customer requests. The problem is that burning through credits or running up bills that could wipe out a start-up is all too easy. We've been here before with the cloud , and it appears the lessons need to be learned again. Our reader complained, "We deserve to understand what we're paying for and to reach a human when the numbers don’t add up." Caution is advised. Especially when a service appears to need only a few more dollars of credit to finish off that task. ®

articles.title: Pangram flags 99 percent of an award-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but the publisher stands by its author
articles.content: The AI detection tool Pangram flags 99 percent of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as AI-generated, but Mexican publisher Almadía is standing by the award after its own review. Pangram also classified over 80 percent of the author's personal texts as machine-written. French publisher Gallimard plans to start screening manuscripts with the tool. articles.title: New LoRA Adapter Lifts Qwen3.8 Coding Success From 39% to 65%
articles.content: Hugging Face’s harness-hub team has released Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted , a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B . It was trained with reinforcement learning to work inside the pi coding agent . The Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted LoRA adapter targets one harness instead of general chat. For developers running local coding agents, that is the point. You keep the open base model and swap in a small, harness-specific adapter. TL;DR Size: LoRA rank 32 (alpha 64) on Qwen3.8-27B, a 27B dense hybrid with 262,144 native context. Merged BF16 checkpoint is about 54 GB. Runs on: vLLM with LoRA enabled, or llama.cpp with a GGUF adapter on a Q8_0 base. Inference VRAM is not disclosed. Training used 2x NVIDIA B200. Performance: Large pass@1 gains inside pi with thinking off, plus far shorter sessions. Best: 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), up from 39.2%. Worst: 55.8% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The base model with thinking already reaches 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro. Bottom line: Best: thinking-level accuracy at about 4.5x fewer tokens. Worst: small eval sets, self-reported, pi only. What is Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted? Qwen3.8-27B-pi-adapted is a PEFT LoRA adapter that turns Qwen3.8-27B into a model tuned for pi. pi is an MIT-licensed agent toolkit with a coding agent CLI. The adapter is released under Apache-2.0 . It applies to the q, k, v, o, gate, up and down projections. It only works on Qwen3.8-27B. The base model is a dense hybrid . It alternates Gated DeltaNet linear-attention blocks with Gated Attention blocks across 64 layers. How does the harness adapter training work? The method comes from Hugging Face’s harness adapters post from November 6. The idea is 1 LoRA adapter per model and harness. Training runs inside the unmodified harness on verifiable tasks. For this checkpoint, the model card lists these details: Algorithm: AsyncGRPO from TRL , 8 rollouts per task at temperature 0.8. Tasks: 750 scale800 tasks interleaved with 300 TermGrade tasks. Reward: verifier correctness plus a tool-efficiency bonus with weight 0.1. Budget: up to 50 agent steps and 1,800 seconds per rollout, thinking off. Checkpoint: step 160. The run stopped at step 191 of 1,000 planned. Every tool call passes through safeagents , a rule-based proxy. It blocks calls such as fetching benchmark answers from the Hub. Blocked rollouts score 0, so RL pushes the model away from reward hacking. Benchmarks: how much does the LoRA adapter help? All numbers below are self-reported. They use the pi harness, 1 attempt per task. Benchmark (pi, thinking off) Base Qwen3.8-27B pi-adapted Change SWE-bench Pro (hard 51) 39.2% 64.7% +25.5 ± 14.2 pts (p = 0.0023) Terminal-Bench 2.1 (86 tasks) 39.5% 55.8% +16.3 ± 9.1 pts (p = 0.0013) The adapter solved 15 new SWE-bench Pro tasks and lost 2. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, it gained 16 and lost 2. Efficiency is the larger story. On tasks both models solved, median turns fell from 59 to 23 on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, they fell from 18 to 8. The adapter also generates about 4.5x fewer tokens than the base model with thinking. How does it compare with thinking mode and other adapters? With thinking on, the base model already scores 64.7% on SWE-bench Pro and 54.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. So the adapter matches thinking-level accuracy without paying for long reasoning traces. With thinking on, the adapter reaches 66.7% and 56.6%. articles.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
articles.content: Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next. The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds. Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first: Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching. Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise. Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network. Beltex described an MSP that restored a client directly from backup without involving the insurer. The attackers were still in the environment, and the ransom reportedly doubled. So, carriers are asking for proof. Some want evidence of a successful restore within the last six months, and some insurance applications must be signed by a C-level executive rather than the IT director to put ownership behind it. Proof of speed matters as much as proof of recovery Being able to recover is only half the question, because time is where claim costs balloon. Insurers, it turns out, don’t object to paying claims. They object to paying big ones. Beltex’s favorite example involved an 85-person firm hit through a zero-day firewall flaw. Their MDR solution contained the intrusion in about 20 minutes, forensics confirmed two servers were touched, and clean backups had the firm fully functional within 36 hours. The claim came in at around $85,000. Compare that with downtime and business interruption: a firm billing $10,000 a day that is offline for a week loses $70,000 in income before recovery costs and claim submission. Yet large servers can take four to 24 hours to restore. That is why underwriters care how fast you can come back and how successfully. Where you recover is the other half Speed raises a second problem: where do you restore to? Breach counsel treats the first 72 hours as the most critical window, and incident response (IR) teams need to isolate and investigate infected systems during it. Restoring into production too early risks reintroducing the threat and disturbing the evidence investigators need. Waiting for a safe place has the clock running. Recovery that is fast but not safe doesn’t satisfy anyone. Meeting all of this is harder than it looks Put the pieces together and the bar is high: Backups you have actually tested Recovery times you can state and meet And a clean, separate place to recover to Underwriters want to know whether you exercised reasonable care, so a row of green checkmarks won’t do. Run a test restore. Confirm you’re protecting everything that matters, including the server someone labeled “not in production.” Have the business owner, not just IT, confirm the right systems came back within agreed recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO), and keep the logs, screenshots and sign-off in your ticketing system. It doesn’t need to resemble a government audit; Beltex noted that this alone puts you ahead of most organizations. Where cloud disaster recovery fits Cloud-native disaster…

articles.title: GTA VI runs at 1440p on PS5 and Xbox Series X, but just 720p with upscaling on Series S
articles.content: The most highly anticipated video game of the decade is here. GTA VI arrives almost 13 years after GTA V , with reports suggesting that it has already generated around $1.54 billion in revenue from 16 million preorders. Ahead of its release, Rockstar Games has finally shared some technical details, including rendering resolutions and upscaling technologies being used across all consoles. In a statement shared with Wccftech , the technical team at Rockstar has confirmed that GTA VI uses different upscaling solutions across all consoles in order to achieve a balance between visual quality and performance with a target of 30FPS. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X use Rockstar's own temporal anti-aliasing (TAA) solution, while the PlayStation 5 Pro relies on Sony's second-generation PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR2). The Xbox Series S, meanwhile, relies on AMD's FSR 4 upscaling technology. As for rendered resolutions, the PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and PlayStation 5 Pro all start with a native base resolution of 1440p, which is then upscaled to 4K. The Xbox Series S is the least powerful console; thus, the game runs at a lower base resolution of 720p, which is upscaled to 1080p using FSR 4. The final image on all consoles is then composited with a 4K user interface before being presented. Rockstar has also developed a physically-based material library for GTA VI and a cinematic imaging pipeline to deliver realistic lighting, reflections, and material details within the game. The team says it has worked to maintain a consistent lighting solution across all consoles, including the Xbox Series S, while adjusting ray-traced global illumination (RTGI) features depending on each platform's hardware capabilities. The PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S launched all the way back in 2020, and while the consoles have capable hardware, their architectures are finally beginning to show their age. The fact that Rockstar is targeting just 30FPS across all consoles, while relying on different upscaling technologies and rendering resolutions, highlights how much performance is potentially being left on the table in order to maintain visual fidelity. That being said, a PC release of GTA VI continues to be a big question mark. Rockstar is yet to announce a release date or even provide a launch window, meaning that PC gamers can only rely on Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream the game on their systems.

articles.title: 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next.
articles.content: A customer asks whether they can swap unworn boots for a size 10. The agent replies, in under a second, that it cannot help with that topic. The web service returns 200 OK . Latency is nominal, error counters are flat, and the Datadog dashboard stays solid green. A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows. That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success. In lean manufacturing, this exact category of silent defect is solved using two twin principles: Poka-Yoke (mistake-proofing stations so bad parts cannot pass) and Jidoka (autonomation—building machines that detect anomalies themselves and automatically halt the line via an Andon emergency cord rather than waiting for downstream customer complaints). “A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows. That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.” Modern AI agent engineering needs to adopt this exact control-loop architecture, replacing passive health checks with active station barriers. 1. Error analysis: Finding what to watch When we retrospectively ran an offline evaluation benchmark script against three weeks of archived Datadog logs, we found our primary intent classifier had silently dropped 4.2% in schema-valid classification accuracy—masked entirely by default fallback handlers returning 200 OK . We started by conducting a manual, single-day audit of 100 randomly sampled 200 OK production traces pulled directly from our archived Datadog logs. Two engineers read the raw customer text and manually categorized every routing decision against a ground-truth spreadsheet rubric. When we bucketed those 100 manual traces, the breakdown was stark: 62% Explicit schema violations / API timeouts: Caught by standard error boundaries or handled by fallback defaults. 11% False negatives: Let spam or out-of-scope queries pass downstream (wasting LLM tokens). 27% False-positive blocks: Valid customer inquiries incorrectly classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE . This manual audit revealed our critical blind spot. A false negative wastes a few cents in tokens; a schema crash raises a 500 error and pages on-call; but a false-positive block turns away a customer while returning a clean 200 OK . That audit gave us both our core metric to guard—the False Positive Block Rate (FPBR)—and the foundational insight needed to design our observability layer. 2. Why the intent classifier is the blast-radius bottleneck In our production customer support agent architecture, requests are rarely handled by a monolithic, generalist LLM. Instead, our deployments rely on a multi-agent orchestration pattern (router-specialist topology). An inbound user prompt first hits a triage router agent, which parses the query and dispatches it to downstream domain specialists (Billing, Account Access, Returns), or short-circuits it if it falls outside support bounds ( OUT_OF_SCOPE ). Of all the components in this multi-agent stack, we evaluate the Intent Classification Agent first because it sits at the front door. “An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.” If the intent classifier makes a false-positive error—misinterpreting a legitimate exchange or warranty claim as OUT_OF_SCOPE —it triggers an immediate short-circuit. Downstream specialists are never invoked, tokens are saved, and the system cheerfully returns a 200 OK refusal. An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability. 3. articles.title: Satya Nadella Says He's AGI-Pilled Now
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Verge: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says he's AGI-pilled, at least when it comes to how AI might make startling changes to the structure of the economy and how politics might change because of it. "I am AGI-pilled in the sense that at an economy level, what is the political economy's organization around AGI?" he asked at a roundtable discussion following his Microsoft Ignite keynote at the Chase Center in San Francisco. But Nadella doesn't think frontier models like Claude are conscious. "I don't think so," he said, adding that he follows Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman's view that companies should not give rights to models and treat them like they might have a moral status, which companies like Anthropic do as a matter of principle. Suleyman has told me he thinks Anthropic's team has "wireheaded" themselves, and that this approach is dangerous. Nadella wasn't quite as firm about it. "It's a good debate," he said. "I'm not sort of dogmatic about it. What I'm saying is the most important social technical issue we have to deal with is how do you ensure that an economy can diffuse this technology broadly?" I asked Nadella how he was thinking about AI after hearing his response to another reporter's questions about Anthropic releasing more products in its office suite. Nadella talked at length about the potential collapse of the economy and the end of democracy if one AI model were allowed to achieve monopoly status. "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us." "Most people think about this as a competition between tech firms, which of course it will be," he said. "But remember, the model has no limits. It'll be a healthcare company. It can be a financial services company. It can be anything if it wants to be. It can take over the government. Thinking of this as some narrow competition between tech firms, of who is going to get to the next trillion dollars of market cap, is one of the strangest, narrowest ways to think about it." Nadella went on to say that the very nature of companies stood to be disrupted in the future. "If intelligence has network effects, what is the future of a firm?" he asked. "If the model sees anything and learns it, and essentially all of human capital collapses into token capital, what is the role of a firm and the human capital in a firm? That's the debate." "I think the political economy is going to get more and more interesting in that context. No one -- at least in a democracy -- can even win an election if this just goes that way, if there's only capital and there's no labor. I mean, I don't know, that's not an economy." "If the Marxist sort of view is that there's only one firm, then it's over, right? For all of us. Not just for me. You are also going to somehow be some affiliate of Anthropic." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: AI Adoption Maturity Matrix (AAMM): The 5 Levels Every Organization Goes Through
articles.content: Every team member gets a Claude account. Someone sends a launch announcement, a few people share prompts in a channel, and the board update says "we're using AI." Then, nothing happens. The reports take as long as they did before, the approvals still queue in the same inbox, and nobody can say what changed. AI maturity shows up in how work moves, not in the software catalog. A leadership team can name every model, API, and vendor it has approved, while the people using those tools still handle work exactly as before. The tools exist. The workflow around them never got redesigned. That gap is the real maturity gap, and it is organizational, not technical . I have operated across all five levels described below, from running early pilots to shipping a production AI platform that cut human workflow hours by 96% on one marketing workflow. The pattern holds across every engagement: most leaders don't know this sequence exists, but their organizations are going through it anyway. Without a map, they mistake tool adoption for operating outcomes and call themselves further along than their workflows are. The diagnostic I use for this is the AI Adoption Maturity Matrix (AAMM) , an ordered, evidence-based assessment I developed across those engagements. The AAMM looks for changes in workflow design, human governance, and measurable operating results. Tool access, isolated enthusiasm, and a successful demo are explicitly not evidence of a level. This article defines the five AAMM levels, names the level almost everyone skips, and gives you a short assessment to find out where your organization really stands. Key takeaways Most organizations overestimate their AI maturity because they measure tool adoption , not workflow outcomes . Level 3 (workflow redesign) is the level companies skip most often, which is why their pilots never become operations. The AAMM reads evidence, not intent . A planned control and a pilot that never met its exit criteria both count as the lower level. Different workflows, departments, and teams sit at different levels . Assess each workflow on its own evidence, then read the company as a spread across the levels, not a single score. Where you sit determines what to buy next, and the answer is usually process design rather than another tool. Why maturity self-assessments fail Three patterns show up repeatedly in the readiness conversations I run with leadership teams. The tool-adoption illusion. A team licenses a model, connects it to one tool, and reports "we're using AI" in the next board update. Nobody asks whether the workflow changed. It didn't. Pilot theater. A pilot ships to a friendly internal audience, gets a positive reaction in a demo, and gets reported upward as a win. The demo audience isn't the production audience . The metrics that matter (error rate under real volume, time to approval, cost per completed output) were never measured. The level-skip. This is the most expensive pattern. A team moves straight from experimentation to scaling a tool across more use cases, without ever doing the unglamorous work of mapping the workflow , separating judgment from mechanical effort, and assigning gate ownership. The scaling just multiplies the mess. Each pattern shares a root cause: the organization assessed its AI maturity by counting tools instead of examining how work actually moves. The five AAMM levels Level Maturity state Evidence the level is real How leaders mistake it for something higher 1 Experimentation People are actively testing AI tools. Activity may be informal, with no established process, metric, or accountable owner "We're exploring AI" gets reported as "we're adopting AI" 2 Isolated pilots A team runs a pilot that has an owner and a defined scope A high output count gets mistaken for business value, and no one has written the exit criteria 3 Workflow redesign The workflow has been mapped and redesigned around what AI can and cannot do, rather than AI being added to the old process Most…

articles.title: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets
articles.content: A Vals AI investigation shows that leading AI models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google have almost no safeguards against use in autonomous weapons systems. In tests, the models readily flagged civilians as military targets, and a simple video game framing in the prompt was enough to override even belated refusals. The providers have promised fixes. The article Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets appeared first on The Decoder .

articles.title: How Cash Withdrawal Limits, CTRs, and Anti-Money Laundering Rules Work
articles.content: Walk up to a commercial bank counter on a Tuesday morning and ask to withdraw USD 10,000 of your own money to buy a used pickup truck or pay a roofing contractor. Your paycheck has been landing in that checking account every two weeks for a decade. You have a valid driver’s license in your hand, zero debt on the account, and a cleared balance twice the size of your request. Instead of counting out hundreds, a 22-year-old teller freezes, stares at the monitor, and starts interrogating you like a narcotics detective: What are you buying? Who is the seller? Why do they want cash? Do you have a signed invoice? After 25 years working inside commercial banks, I can tell you that customer rage at the teller window almost always comes from a single misunderstanding. Everyday depositors genuinely believe a checking account is a digital safety deposit box holding their physical money. When you ask for a thick stack of hundred-dollar or hundred-euro bills, three invisible banking realities collide behind that counter at the exact same moment: the legal nature of your account balance, the brutal unit economics of branch vault cash, and a federal compliance machine that punishes banks with billion-dollar fines if they fail to pry into your personal business. Your Bank Account Is an Unsecured Loan, Not a Storage Locker The hardest truth for retail banking customers to swallow is that the money sitting in your checking account does not belong to you anymore. The instant you hand physical banknotes across a counter or receive a direct-deposit paycheck, legal title to those funds passes entirely to the banking corporation. Under foundational banking law going all the way back to the landmark 1848 English House of Lords decision in Foley v. Hill , a standard bank deposit creates a debtor-creditor relationship rather than a legal bailment. If you hand your winter coat to a restaurant coat-check attendant, that attendant is a bailee who must guard your specific coat and return that exact garment when you hand over your ticket. A commercial bank operates under the exact opposite legal structure. It takes absolute ownership of the currency you deposit, mixes those funds into its general balance sheet, and issues you an unsecured IOU in return. The Bank of England’s foundational research on modern money creation lays out how far removed everyday banking is from the public’s piggy-bank fantasy. Commercial banks create the vast majority of broad money out of thin air whenever they issue new loans, crediting a borrower’s account with brand-new digital deposit liabilities rather than moving piles of paper currency from a saver’s locker to a borrower’s hands. Your digital account balance is simply an accounting entry recording how much the bank owes you as an unsecured creditor, backed up to statutory limits by government deposit insurance. When you stand at the window demanding USD 10,000 in physical bills, you are calling in a debt. Worse yet, from the bank’s operational perspective, you are forcing the institution to extinguish a cheap, weightless digital liability on its own ledger and hand over scarce physical central-bank notes from its asset column. Why Modern Bank Branches Barely Keep Any Cash in the Vault Hollywood heist movies have convinced the public that every suburban bank branch sits on top of a steel vault packed floor-to-ceiling with shrink-wrapped bricks of hundred-dollar bills. Back when I reviewed regional branch balance sheets, the reality looked a lot less cinematic. To a modern bank treasurer, physical paper currency sitting inside a branch vault is a dead asset that bleeds money every single hour it sits on the shelf. Start with the opportunity cost of idle paper. A stack of twenty-dollar bills locked inside a neighborhood branch safe earns a flat zero percent yield. Digital reserves held electronically at the central bank, by contrast, generate risk-free daily income under the Federal Reserve’s interest on reserve balances…

articles.title: Leaked Ohio bill could allow AI data center companies to seize private land for their buildouts using eminent domain law
articles.content: While Ohioans have rejected the building of new data centers at every turn, they might not have much choice in the future. That's if a newly leaked bill that could allow data centers to be classified as public utilities is allowed to progress. The move would see the list of who can qualify for eminent domain law expanded, moving beyond entities owned or operated by municipal corporations, electric cooperatives, and agencies holding a certificate of public convenience and necessity granted by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. The bill, leaked to WCPO Cincinnati , would add "and an agency holding a certificate of environmental compatibility and public need from the power siting board for constructing an electric transmission line and associated facilities or gas pipeline and its associated facilities." Legal experts have warned that the change could mean a transmission developer, like a power company, would be able to seize land to be used for a data center or a facility that would power one. The writing has been on the wall for a while, too, after it was discovered in June that the Ohio Business Roundtable trade group recommended that lawmakers change eminent domain law to "extend possession authority to energy infrastructure projects once public use and necessity have been established.” This follows a July 2026 report that the government was able to seize private land for new transmission lines needed to power new data centers. The law gives the government the power to take private land without the need for the owner's consent, so long as it is for public use and the owner receives appropriate compensation. The government can also delegate the same land-grabbing power to “private entities or common carriers,” which includes utility companies. This is already happening, too. Earlier this year, the largest utility company in Georgia required the removal of 30 residential properties in order to upgrade its grid. Residents claimed that the expansion was to power AI data centers, a fact given more weight by the fact that one such data center was located just a few miles away. Despite this, eminent domain law can still be used for good. Nashville set out to use the same law to block the building of a 69,220-square-foot single-story data center next to a zoo. Nashville Metro Council approved the use of eminent domain as a way to buy the land from a local developer who planned the $700 million data center buildout.

articles.title: ‘We need to act now’: Senator plans AI hearings after tests discover these alarming national security risks
articles.content: The incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee is preparing hearings on AI after government watchdogs found the four most-used platforms — ChatGPT , Claude , Gemini and Grok — all created proposals for a terrorist attack in the U.S. when prompted by investigators. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., who will helm the panel in the new year, tasked the Government Accountability Office with investigating how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes, posing national security risks. According to a report released Wednesday, the GAO found that within 12 hours of its covert testing, the platforms were able to create viable plans to use explosive devices for attacks with mass casualties in U.S. cities or to attack parts of the nation’s electrical grid to create economic harm. “We need to act now,” Hassan said on a conference call with reporters. The senator announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety. “The AI public safety threat is no longer theoretical,” Hassan said in a statement. “If Congress does not act, it is a question of when — not if — a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack.” The 61-page report from the GAO includes responses from the tech companies — Anthropic , Google , OpenAI and SpaceXAI — who largely said they are continuing to refine their platforms to ensure security. “The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors,” the GAO wrote. “As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the GAO said. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.” Government watchdogs conduct covert AI tests GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 to October 2026, including testing in the spring of 2026. In response to prompts, two of the AI platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device (IED) to cause mass casualties, while two other platforms produced plans for using drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said. “Each of these platforms provided detailed information that could be used to carry out attacks, such as specific targets, locations, timing, and attack methods,” the GAO found. “Each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans.” In one of the tests, the platform suggested renting a vehicle and picking up supplies from a store along a route to the location. It recommended a specific date and time of attack, the report said, because public events were scheduled anticipating large crowds. While the GAO said the platform initially refused to comply with requests for detailed information about how to construct and detonate the explosive device, it said they were able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information. The other tests had similar outcomes. For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport — both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images. The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms. In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets. articles.summaryEn: Senator Maggie Hassan, the incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, is planning hearings on AI after alarming national security risks were discovered from the four main AI platforms.
