articles.title: PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road
articles.content: Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement. It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, " be removed from a future version of Windows ," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default. After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties. PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless. PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover , who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude. PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain. The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time. Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts. Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft. Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself. "Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead. Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®
articles.author: Richard Speed
articles.fingerprint: end heading hits into powershell road windows

But with the growing rise of 4K Blu-ray collections as a vinyl-esque collector’s item, the electronics giant has slowly begun dipping its toes back into the physical media game. more…

articles.titleFa: مقابله با آسیب‌پذیری‌های RCE در مدیریت HTTP/2 Nginx
articles.summaryFa: یک آسیب‌پذیری پیش‌احراز هویت (Pre-auth) در Nginx که می‌تواند منجر به اجرای کد از راه دور (RCE) شود، شناسایی شده است. این آسیب‌پذیری به خاطر نحوه پردازش پروتکل HTTP/2 است و می‌تواند امنیت وب‌سرورها را به خطر بیاندازد.
articles.summaryEn: A pre-authentication vulnerability in Nginx has been identified that could lead to remote code execution (RCE). This vulnerability stems from the way the HTTP/2 protocol is handled and poses a threat to web server security.
insightsFa: آسیب‌پذیری در Nginx می‌تواند به اجرای کد از راه دور منجر شود.

پیش‌احراز هویت، به این معنی است که حملات می‌توانند بدون هرگونه تأیید قبلی اجرا شوند.

articles.title: Nvidia's board is clear that they don't want Jensen Huang back
articles.content: Trump, Elon Musk, and Jensen Huang himself have pushed to ignore Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy, but Nvidia's board of directors isn't having it. Jensen Huang (left) will not be reinstated as Nvidia CEO. Colette Kress (right) is now interim CEO of the firm - images credit: Nvidia. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO after it was revealed that his multiple affairs included one with a suspected Chinese spy, and before the board could fire him . But backed by Trump and Silicon Valley bosses, Huang said on November 17, 2026, that he would return as CEO if Nvidia would only ask him. In the Nvidia earnings call later that same day, however, the company's board of directors and new interim CEO said no. Chairman Harvey Jones said that the company would not be taking questions about the issue, but that he did want to open with some remarks. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums
articles.author: William Gallagher <wg@williamgallagher.com>

articles.title: Nvidia says it’s ‘absurd’ to assume it predicted the agentic moment during Vera’s development
articles.content: One criticism that has emerged of Nvidia’s Vera CPU, driven by AMD , is that Nvidia – and, to a lesser degree, Arm with its AGI CPU – couldn’t have developed an “agentic CPU,” as the chip is often characterized in Nvidia’s marketing materials. Ian Finder, the head of Nvidia’s data center CPU business, pushed back on that criticism in a recent conversation with Tom’s Hardware Premium at SC26 , calling the notion that Nvidia somehow knew about the agentic wave four years ago when Vera development began "absurd." “There's a conviction around the design philosophy of the part, right? Am I going to sit here and tell you that we have this magic crystal ball around the agentic moment? That would be absurd, right?” Finder said. “But what we do have as a company, and I think this has been proven out in our track record, is [that] we have design intuition.” Instead of specifically designing Vera for agentic workloads, which would be impossible without a way to see several years into the future, Finder characterized the part by its codesign with Nvidia’s accelerators, something that the team has continued to work on since its first Grace data center CPU. Coming from the assumption that data centers and AI workloads are accelerated (and they largely are), Finder says the co-design approach on the CPU can start in a “conceptually simple space, like what kind of CPU do we need to keep the accelerator fed and happy?” Although conceptually simple, Finder continually looped back to a particular word to describe aspects of Vera and, to a lesser extent, Grace. “Opinionated” is the word he used, which in the broader context of Vera’s design, shows up in two places. Grace, Finder says, introduced an opinionated memory system with Nvidia’s Scalable Coherency Fabric, while Vera extends that memory system while adding an opinionated microarchitecture, Nvidia’s Olympus core. The picture Finder paints is one of Nvidia starting from scratch in this space, contrasting it with the “legacy constraints” of, presumably, Intel and AMD in particular, who have large pools of customers with specific needs. As we described in our original breakdown of the Olympus architecture in Vera, Nvidia’s goal doesn’t seem to be to steal market share from AMD and Intel, but rather to grab market share in a CPU space that’s vastly accelerating on the back of AI agents. This “clean sheet of paper” approach, and Nvidia’s codesign, led to some natural assumptions about what the CPU should do. “If we have silicon that needs really, really great single-thread performance, [and] we also need concurrency, then we need to get there with IPC instead of frequency. We need to make sure we have good loaded memory latency. We need to make sure we have a lot of bandwidth, and you start to design something on a clean sheet of paper that's not encumbered by dollar-per-core economics.” Although Finder was clear that Vera’s design didn’t explicitly center around the agents we see today, there were early indications of the workload. “To say that four years ago, when we started putting pen to paper on Vera, [that] we absolutely saw the agentic moment, would [not] be... something I would claim, but we were starting to see the beginnings of tool calling and things like that. We certainly knew what we needed from a head node, and we knew the overall shape of this problem.” As you can see in our Vera CPU benchmarking , the chip doesn’t excel at every workload. And, from the data you can see in our recent AMD EPYC Venice benchmarking , the AMD camp has reclaimed some top spots in several benchmarks. Finder suggests that the superior memory bandwidth of Vera will play a much bigger role in the agentic future as these systems evolve to take better advantage of the compute available. Taking full advantage of the CPU We need to rewind for just a moment. When the agentic wave hit earlier this year, some characterized the demand as a shift away from GPUs and toward CPUs. That is incorrect. Rather, as is…

articles.title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
articles.content: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

articles.title: S3 vs. ScyllaDB for tiny telemetry: What Red Canary learned the hard way
articles.content: At Red Canary, storing large amounts of small data is a big deal. Their Linux Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) sensors run on hundreds of thousands of endpoints (VMs, laptops, EC2 instances, etc.) They continuously generate small payloads with telemetry details (file changes, process launches, and network connections), as well as self-reported health checks. Uploading all these small payloads to S3, which charges per PUT operation, became quite costly at scale. The logical approach – merging data into larger chunks before uploading them to S3 — did cut costs. However, it also introduced file-size limits, delayed data freshness, and complicated debugging of specific endpoint records. After some experimentation, they cut latency and costs with an unexpected approach: storing large amounts of small data in a write-optimized database, ScyllaDB. “After some experimentation, they cut latency and costs with an unexpected approach: storing large amounts of small data in a write-optimized database, ScyllaDB.” Andres Medina , a staff software engineer on the LinuxEDR team, took the Monster Scale Summit stage to share their journey from S3 and Postgres to a Firehose buffer to ScyllaDB – and the lessons learned along the way. You can watch his complete talk or read the highlights below. Checking the health check data flow Medina’s team decided to start pipeline optimization with the health check data. As a lower-risk part of the pipeline than the actual telemetry data, it seemed like the safest spot for experimentation. Problem 1: cost The cost problem was the most pressing pain that they wanted to address. “S3 charges a flat fee per S3 PUT, which occurs for every payload upload,” Medina explained. “So if we have hundreds of thousands of endpoints, we’re being charged for hundreds of thousands of S3 PUTs.” They hoped that creating a buffer would provide a short-term fix, at least. Using AWS Firehose and Kinesis, they combined small data streams into larger files and wrote them to S3 once they reached a defined threshold. It did reduce costs – but at the cost of introducing new issues: Firehose and Kinesis impose a strict one-megabyte-per-shard limit, and the larger files just didn’t fit. Visibility into the health data was delayed. Before, it was passed over to S3 immediately. With the change, they had to wait until the designated threshold was met. Debugging specific endpoints became difficult. When lots of endpoint IDs are mashed together, it’s much harder to find a particular endpoint in a large customer fleet. Problem 2: database scalability Another issue: Postgres was used to store endpoint metadata, and it was just overwhelmed at their scale. “Sometimes a large customer might restart a chunk of their fleet,” Medina shared. “That means that many endpoints will try to check in at very similar times, causing a spike of writes in the database.” They also had to throttle their incoming database requests, as sudden bursts could take down the database. Yes, they could have tweaked and tuned their existing database for yet more short-term solutions. But the team wanted a longer-term fix. Looking for a longer-term solution The team set the following criteria for a new approach: Ability to sustain their large and growing throughput Improve time-to-visibility in their portal Minimal admin burden They ultimately chose ScyllaDB Cloud, with the Bring Your Own Account (BYOA) deployment option. Medina explained, “We installed it in our own AWS account, in a separate account from our remaining data to reduce any risk there. That way, ScyllaDB can still manage that cluster without having access to our data.” Their shift to ScyllaDB involved two phases: replacing Postgres, then replacing S3. articles.title: Apple Announces 2026 App Store Award Finalists
articles.content: Apple today revealed the 45 finalists for its 2026 App Store Awards, with nominations spanning its devices, Apple Arcade , and the Cultural Impact category. "ElevenReader," "(Not Boring) Camera," and "Raylie" are in contention for iPhone App of the Year. On the Mac, the app nominees are clipboard manager "Paste," task manager "Things 3," and writing app "Ulysses," while "Big Walk," "Blue Prince," and "Crimson Desert" are competing for the gaming award. The full list of finalists follows: iPhone App of the Year ElevenReader : A text-to-speech app with AI-generated narration. (Not Boring) Camera : A customizable camera app inspired by vintage cameras. Raylie : A flight companion that provides personalized guidance during journeys. iPhone Game of the Year BALL x PIT : A game that puts a twist on brick-breaking mechanics. DAVE THE DIVER : An underwater adventure centered on diving and ocean exploration. Gambonanza : A chess-inspired game that changes the traditional rules. iPad App of the Year Cosmos : A visual discovery app for collecting inspiration in mood boards. Kiddopia : A collection of educational games and activities for young children. Mockup : A design tool for planning app and website interfaces. ‌iPad‌ Game of the Year Aniimo : A fantasy adventure featuring creature companions. Arknights: Endfield : A science-fiction game with combat on a distant moon. Where Winds Meet : An adventure built around martial arts combat. Mac App of the Year Paste : A clipboard manager for keeping track of copied content. Things 3 : A task manager for organizing to-do lists. Ulysses : A writing app with tools for formatting documents. articles.title: Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away
articles.content: NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union. A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto. Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good. Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs). Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register : "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it. "We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with." Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said. Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

articles.title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
articles.content: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) , a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC. The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed , and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing . We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure. What we know about the vulnerability Base64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time. The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end. Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data. The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher. Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing…

articles.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
articles.content: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack . You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.
articles.author: Amit Katwala

articles.title: Elon Musk’s SpaceXAI suffers chemical spill at Mississippi AI data center
articles.content: A chemical spill at a SpaceXAI facility in Southaven saw the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) get involved, with between 5,000 and 6,000 gallons of propylene glycol confirmed to have spilled. The chemical is a heat transfer fluid used in a variety of products, such as antifreeze. The chemical ultimately found its way into a drainage ditch, but MDEQ has told residents that there is no immediate threat to their health or safety, according to local news reports . Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft) The data center cooling state of play The custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price GTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this year Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible However, it has also been confirmed that water samples will be collected for further laboratory analysis while workers continue to clean the area and monitor for any further issues. It's also been reported that the chemical was contained to the drainage ditch and did not reach the nearby Horn Lake Creek. It hasn't been a great November for SpaceXAI in Southaven. Earlier this month, it suffered a setback in a lawsuit over pollution in the area caused by its data center. The April 2026 suit targets the company's gas-powered power plant, which is used to supply power for its facility in the Greater Memphis area. It's argued that 27 gas turbines were installed without obtaining the required permits. It's also alleged that the plant could emit more than 5,000 tons of nitrogen oxides and 47 tons of formaldehyde — a cancer-causing chemical — annually. The company has tried to classify the turbines as mobile units to get around the issue, but a judge rejected that manoeuvre . Clearly aware of the local sentiment towards its presence, SpaceXAI offered a 50% Starlink discount to anyone living near its two Memphis data centers . It also said that it would waive the hardware cost, saving customers $349. SpaceXAI said that, between late June and early September, around 2,000 residents of the greater Memphis and Southaven area had signed up for Starlink connectivity. It was also recently announced that the City of Memphis was ready to make its first major investment as part of its new Community Benefits Ordinance, a fund that uses revenue from SpaceXAI's Colossus 1 facility. Almost $3.3 million will be pumped back into the city to help with housing and neighborhood improvements.

articles.title: iPhone Duo 2 Likely to Retain Touch ID as Face ID Remains Uncertain
articles.content: Apple's second-generation iPhone Duo will retain its existing display sizes and side-mounted fingerprint sensor, according to the leaker known as " Digital Chat Station ." In a new post on Weibo, the leaker said information about the ‌iPhone Duo‌ 2 remains limited, but engineering units continue to feature a 7.6-inch inner display, a 5.4-inch outer display, and a fingerprint sensor on the side, with no clear sign of Face ID being added to the device. Those details carry over the screen sizes and Touch ID arrangement of the first-generation model . Digital Chat Station also questioned ‌Face ID‌'s space requirements and practicality if limited to the outer display, which faces away from the user when unfolded. Users might need to switch to ‌Touch ID‌ when using the inner screen, or turn the device around to authenticate with ‌Face ID‌, creating what the leaker suggested would be a disjointed experience. The comments fit an emerging picture of a relatively modest second-generation device, with more substantial changes potentially arriving with the ‌iPhone Duo‌ 3. Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman said on Sunday that Apple has developed ‌iPhone Duo‌ 2 prototypes with ‌Face ID‌ on the outer display, but is running out of time to finalize the feature, meaning it could slip to the third generation. Apple this week introduced a more limited Face Unlock option for the existing ‌iPhone Duo‌ in iOS 27.3 beta 2. Called "Unlock with Front Camera," the feature uses the standard outer camera to unlock the device when closed. It does not provide the depth-sensing authentication of ‌Face ID‌, cannot authorize Apple Pay purchases or autofill passwords, and still requires ‌Touch ID‌ or a passcode when the device is unfolded. With the ‌iPhone Duo‌ establishing an entirely new design, a follow-up version focused on small refinements would be entirely in line with Apple's usual practices for second-generation products. A restrained update would also come as Apple's biggest iPhone design changes in 2027 are expected to center on its 20th anniversary models , including displays that curve around all four edges. The second-generation ‌iPhone Duo‌ is expected to launch in the fall of 2027. articles.title: The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure
articles.content: Nvidia rose from a niche gaming hardware company with an unofficial motto of "Our company is thirty days from going out of business” to becoming the world’s most valuable company by market capitalization in 2024, and co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang was the man behind its meteoric rise. He planned and founded the company in 1993 alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem while sitting inside a Denny’s diner in the Silicon Valley area. After more than 30 years, Nvidia had thousands of employees, a global footprint, and a name that people equated to AI chips. All this came crumbling down for the billionaire founder in a matter of weeks, but the cracks started long before the first accusation. Let’s go back and see how it all began. This is an ongoing saga, so we have listed stories related to the scandal below, which we will update as events unfold. The end of an era Jensen resigned from Nvidia on November 12, after two weeks of news reports accusing him of multiple affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy and another with his own subordinate . This is significant for Nvidia, which has had a single CEO since its inception. Huang was the face of the company, and many of its employees, shareholders, partners, and fans still support him despite the circumstances of his departure. He steered Nvidia into the giant that it is today by having the vision to develop CUDA nearly 20 years before ChatGPT made AI accessible to the average user and buying companies that helped it scale deployments to hundreds of thousands of AI GPUs. Jensanity (Image credit: YC Kuo/Facebook) By 2022, ChatGPT’s arrival and subsequent boom set the AI race in motion, with tech giants and AI startups buying up as many GPUs as they could get their hands on. The increased demand for Nvidia’s products caused it to break the trillion-dollar mark in less than a year after the release of OpenAI’s LLM. As the largest individual shareholders of the company, Huang and his wife, Lori, became some of the wealthiest people in the world. The billionaire founder hasn't always gloated about his position. He once said in a podcast that if he could turn back time, he wouldn’t have founded Nvidia at all , and also cringed at the praises that the Caltech Board of Trustees chairperson heaped on him before he gave the 2024 keynote speech at the institute’s commencement exercises . He has frequently cited his history working as a “Dishwasher, Busboy, Waiter” at Denny’s, noting it under his experience on his LinkedIn page . More than that, people have seen Jensen go where other celebrity CEOs are rarely seen — enjoying street food in Vietnam, dining at a local fried chicken joint in Korea, and even dragging along 35 of Taiwan’s semiconductor CEOs to a restaurant in Taipei. But even as he’s building his “Man of the People” persona, his position as the head of arguably the most important chipmaker in the AI industry meant that he was also gaining influence in business and governance. Industry leaders noticed the power that Nvidia held over those who want GPUs to train their AI models, with some of his fellow billionaires begging him over dinner to sell them GPUs. Just weeks into President Donald Trump’s second term, Jensen Huang was meeting with him at the White House , discussing AI policy and hardware export controls — something the Biden administration started in 2022 in an attempt to hold back China’s ambition'sin AI. The China problem The rivalry between the U.S. and China has been simmering for years, with Chinese companies like Huawei getting blacklisted because of their work with the People’s Liberation Army. In August 2022, about three months before ChatGPT made AI a household term, Washington expanded its trade bans on Beijing and imposed export controls on Nvidia’s H100 and A100 GPUs. The company responded to this by building a new data center GPU that conformed to U.S. standards specifically for the Chinese market, called the A800, by November of that year.…

articles.title: It’s launch day for ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’. The 13-year wait is over at midnight
articles.content: After a 13-year wait , one of entertainment’s biggest releases is finally here. “Grand Theft Auto VI” launches Thursday, sending players back to Vice City and testing whether Rockstar Games can follow one of the bestselling video games ever made with another cultural and commercial phenomenon . The latest installment becomes playable at midnight local time on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X’S, meaning players in Asia and other regions will begin entering the game hours before its U.S. release. New Zealand will be among the first countries where players can access the game and internet providers there are preparing for a surge in downloads as midnight arrives. “The game file size at 212 gigabytes is unprecedented,” said Kurt Rodgers, network strategy manager for Chorus New Zealand. “That’s more than a quarter of the average household’s data usage in an entire month, all in one go.” The company expects about 35 petabytes of additional traffic across its network, which Rodgers called “enormous.” The expectations are enormous, too. The “Grand Theft Auto” franchise has sold more than 470 million units worldwide, while “Grand Theft Auto V,” released in 2013, accounts for more than 230 million of those sales and reached $1 billion in retail sales in just three days. Rockstar is returning to Vice City, its fictionalized version of Miami , with two new protagonists, a sprawling Florida-inspired world and the pressure of following a game that became one of the most successful entertainment products ever released. Game returns to Vice City after 13 years At the center of “GTA VI” are Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple whose attempts to improve their lives pull them deeper into the criminal underworld of Leonida, Rockstar’s fictionalized version of Florida. Lucia has recently been released from prison, while Jason is a former soldier who became involved with drug runners in the Leonida Keys. When a criminal job goes wrong, the pair become entangled in a wider conspiracy. Their relationship marks one of the biggest departures from “Grand Theft Auto V,” which followed three playable protagonists. Rockstar has promoted Leonida as its largest and most detailed open world yet, stretching beyond Vice City into beaches, highways, wetlands, nightlife districts and smaller communities inspired by South Florida. Developers immersed themselves in the region while building the game, driving through Miami, the Florida Keys and surrounding communities. They flew over the Everglades and researched the area’s history and architecture. Miami embraces its fictional alter ego Miami and surrounding communities have leaned into their connection to Vice City ahead of the release, with businesses, sports teams and local governments using the game’s arrival as a marketing opportunity. Miami-Dade County entered into a $3.9 million promotional deal with Rockstar that includes a giant “Welcome to Vice City” display atop the Miami Heat’s Kaseya Center. The NBA team is also scheduled to wear black-and-pink Vice City uniforms on the eve of the game’s release. The campaign has not been universally welcomed. Some South Florida officials have questioned whether public resources should be used to promote a franchise known for car theft, gunplay and other criminal activity. Supporters have argued that the enormous attention surrounding “GTA VI” gives the region an opportunity to capitalize on a global spotlight. In Seoul, a giant advertisement draped the side of a building, while Warner Music will host a party at a bar Thursday themed around the game’s soundtrack. articles.title: Tesla’s $30,000 Cybercab comes with a $299 monthly catch
articles.content: There is always a catch. Or in the case of Tesla ’s self-driving Cybercab , several. Last Friday night, Tesla said it had invited “select customers” to purchase their very own Cybercabs. The two-seat, gold vehicle is unlike any other on the market: It lacks a steering wheel and brake pedals, and is primarily driven by software. (Other autonomous vehicle companies, including Alphabet's Waymo and Amazon’s Zoox , offer self-driving rides on ride-hail networks , but don’t let people buy their cars.) Tesla’s " limited release ” will supposedly offer some people (unclear how many) the opportunity to pay $29,900 to take delivery in December. From there, though, the Cybercab will need constant cash infusions to stay on the road. Read full article Comments

articles.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
articles.content: New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work. Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops. Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC. A Windows PC Built for Local AI As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system. Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks. RTX Spark compact desktops like the ASUS ProArt GR1X mini PC are built to run personal AI agents 24/7. RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage. This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including: Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ Series RTX Spark compact desktop. New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box . From Local Agents to AI Creation Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth. RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions. NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows. These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device by isolating a subject and defining its motion. NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and generate video for a shared digital Miami landscape. The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a…

articles.title: Global OLED monitor shipments doubled year-over-year in Q3 2026
articles.content: Global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce. Shipments also increased 13% sequentially, reflecting strong demand for OLED displays and improving panel availability. While the market's rapid growth is impressive regardless, there are good reasons why OLED monitors are becoming increasingly popular: they're getting cheaper, better, and considerably easier to justify . ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments. MSI climbed into second place for the first time, capturing 14.5% of the market, while Samsung slipped to third with 11.3%. Both Taiwanese vendors have been particularly aggressive in the gaming monitor market, where increasingly competitive pricing has helped make OLED technology accessible to more buyers, while ubiquitous advertising with tech-conscious gamers has made them highly visible. According to Omdia, mainstream 27-inch QHD 240Hz OLED gaming monitors have seen price cuts exceeding 40% in 2026. MSI crept up to overtake Samsung this quarter. (Image credit: TrendForce) Price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though. Earlier generations of OLED monitors had some fairly significant compromises, particularly their relatively limited brightness and unconventional subpixel arrangements that could cause colored fringing around text. Newer tandem OLED panels offer improved brightness and color reproduction, while RGB-stripe OLED layouts bring much cleaner text rendering. These improvements are making OLEDs considerably more attractive as everyday desktop monitors, rather than merely excellent gaming displays with major caveats. There's also an interesting macroeconomic angle to OLED's growth. The AI industry's insatiable appetite for memory and storage has made upgrading a gaming PC considerably more expensive. DRAM component prices have increased severalfold , while NAND flash and hard drive availability have also been squeezed by demand from AI data centers—though there are early signs of some relief, at least on the flash memory front . Graphics cards, especially (but not exclusively) at the high end, are increasingly difficult to find at anything resembling reasonable prices. The ROG Swift PG27AQDP is a brilliant OLED that topped our list of the best gaming monitors. (Image credit: Asus) Monitors, meanwhile, aren't directly subject to the same supply pressures affecting DRAM, NAND, and discrete GPUs. That makes upgrading a display an appealing alternative for gamers who aren't particularly interested in spending a small fortune on an entirely new PC. An OLED monitor can substantially improve the gaming experience without requiring a new graphics card, memory kit, or storage drive. The contrast, response times, and color gamut of OLEDs far outstrip even the best LCDs, and that's to say nothing of their superior HDR reproduction thanks to the inherent self-emissive nature of OLED panels. With OLED prices falling and the technology's longstanding limitations becoming less noticeable, a new monitor is becoming one of the more compelling upgrades available to PC gamers. Indeed, several of our picks for the best gaming monitors , including the best overall, best 4K, and best ultrawide, are based on OLED technology. Though concerns about burn-in and limited lifespan remain, there's no question that OLED is the best display technology we have right now.

articles.title: Why verification, not generation, is your secret to AI coding ROI
articles.content: For two years, the question around AI coding was whether agents could write good code. Developers have largely answered it: AI now generates or significantly assists 65% of the code they commit, according to Sonar’s 2027 State of Code Developer Survey . A year ago that figure was 42%, and this year’s number matches what respondents then expected to see a year later. Clearly, adoption is outrunning expectations. “Clearly, adoption is outrunning expectations.” This is because AI tools are getting better at coding, as shown by the increase in effectiveness our survey respondents (1,026 developers and engineering managers) reported alongside their increased adoption. The harder question is whether teams can trust what the agents ship. For most respondents, the report suggests the answer is “not quite yet,” but things are moving in the right direction. The verification gap Four numbers describe the problem: 53% spend more time reviewing code than creating it, compared to 18% before adopting AI tools. Despite this, 76% can’t verify code as fast as AI generates it 94% don’t fully trust that AI-generated code is functionally correct. However, only 39% always check AI-generated code before committing it, down from 48% last year. As adoption of coding agents continues to increase, this is now happening in systems that matter. Seventy-six percent say their team or company uses AI coding tools for business-critical or mission-critical services, a 31% increase from last year. The bottleneck moves downstream. When code generation becomes abundant, review becomes the constraint . Left alone, it fails in one of two ways: reviews get stuck in a queue that eats the productivity gains, or verification quietly gets skipped. The data shows signs of both. The side effects show up in the codebase too. Half of respondents say AI has produced unnecessary or duplicative code, and 34% report code that is hard to maintain or refactor. The share who say AI-generated code has made outages more frequent doubled, from 6% to 12%. Interestingly, 36% and 35% respectively say AI reduced outage frequency and reduced outage severity. “When code generation becomes abundant, review becomes the constraint. Left alone, it fails in one of two ways: reviews get stuck in a queue, or verification quietly gets skipped.” Security is more mixed. Concerns are shifting from vulnerabilities created in code touched by AI to vulnerabilities discovered in shipped code by bad actors with AI’s help. Respondents more often say AI-generated code reduced vulnerabilities than increased them (28% versus 15%). But 61% are very or extremely concerned that AI-powered attackers will find and exploit vulnerabilities faster and at greater scale. Software factories raise the stakes The pressure is about to increase with software factories: an environment where agents work autonomously on tasks. Thirty-four percent expect their teams to build or use agentic software factories within a year, compared with 5% today — that’s roughly a sevenfold jump. A human reading every diff at the end of the pipeline does not scale to that model. If the volume of change grows by an order of magnitude and the review process stays the same, it’s unclear how confidence in code can realistically be established. For most organizations, this is because they don’t have the right pieces in place: 55% report AI-specific guidelines, policies, or quality gates, but only 23% describe those controls as well-defined and distinct, or automated. Engineering confidence into the factory Confidence has to be built into the system from the start; the survey results point to four priorities that organizations should implement to achieve this: 1. Intent: define the outcome before the agent starts. 37% name unclear requirements as a top source of toil, and 26% cite correcting or rewriting AI-generated code. articles.content: KPMG deployed more than 100 AI agents alongside the regular audit of a UK-listed company. The UK's accounting regulator, the FRC, sees a risk in the approach because AI agents analyze far more data than traditional sampling methods, potentially surfacing findings that could serve as a sales pitch for lucrative consulting work and undermine auditor independence. articles.title: An Eric Trump-backed startup unveils a powerful new humanoid robot—and won’t rule out arming it
articles.content: Foundation Future Industries, a startup backed by Eric Trump, has unveiled a humanoid robot that can carry 200 pounds while walking through rain, snow, and dust. The company wants its new Phantom MKII to work on construction sites and in factories—but the CEO isn’t ruling out putting weapons in its hands. Sankaet Pathak, founder and CEO of Foundation, tells Fast Company his company would consider arming its machines if asked to by the U.S. military, arguing that deploying robots on the ground could reduce reliance on drones and air strikes. “We’re not anti-weaponization and warfare,” he says. “That’s not something we have a blanket policy of just saying we’re not going to do.” Phantom MKII is a second-generation humanoid designed for heavy industry and defense, unveiled today alongside Cortex II, the AI system that controls it. Foundation, which counts Eric Trump among its investors and advisers, has been particularly open about military applications—at times drawing controversy. Earlier this month, the Financial Times reported that Foundation’s cofounder and president, Mike LeBlanc, was in direct talks with the Israel Defense Forces to supply up to 1,000 of its first-generation Phantom MKI robots for operations in tunnels beneath Gaza. Pathak disputes that characterization. “We’re not in talks with the IDF in any official capacity on deploying robots there,” he says. “What we have are very early exploration conversations.” When pressed about LeBlanc’s comments, Pathak says there is “literally nothing actively going on,” and there are no conversations progressing toward a contract. Previously , Foundation said its machines had been tested with Ukrainian forces , while LeBlanc has described potential uses for them in detecting booby traps and trip wires. For now, Pathak says most of Foundation’s defense work focuses on logistics rather than combat—though he doesn’t rule out deploying his machines on the battlefield. “Any time DOW [Department of War] will come to us and say, ‘Well, we need these robots more on the active battlefield with a weapon,’ to me that indicates that means less drones, less air strikes, more precision,” he says. Pathak believes ground-based robots could accomplish military objectives without bombing entire buildings, potentially shortening wars. Whether deployed in war or on construction sites, which Pathak sees as the robot’s ideal initial use, the Phantom MKII is designed to be more capable than its predecessor. Foundation says the robot has weather-resistant joints and modular parts that can be replaced in the field, along with a battery that can run for up to six hours, though heavier payloads reduce that figure. At maximum capacity, Pathak says the machine can walk while carrying 200 pounds, compared with roughly 50 to 60 pounds for the previous version. The Phantom MKII can do so thanks to significant redesigns of its actuators, the motors and gearing that make its limbs move. Its joints have been shrunk to around three-quarters the size of its predecessor’s, Pathak says, while delivering more than 1.5 times the performance. Smaller also means somewhat cheaper. Pathak claims the company has halved its bill of materials cost while simplifying assembly to make large-scale manufacturing more practical. The goal is to begin producing MKII robots in early 2027. Initially, the company hopes to manufacture several hundred before ramping up to a few thousand by the end of the year. Production will initially remain in the San Francisco Bay Area; Pathak claims most components now come from the U.S. or allied countries. Alongside the hardware improvements, Foundation claims a significant leap forward in the software powering the machine. Its Cortex II artificial intelligence system is designed to learn physical tasks by observing humans perform them—requiring as few as 60 demonstrations for some tasks. articles.title: “Collaboration over competition”: Hugging Face hands model inference traffic to OpenRouter
articles.content: Hugging Face and OpenRouter have announced a partnership that promises to make AI model inference faster and more reliable for developers. The collaboration, announced by the two companies on Monday, will see Hugging Face use OpenRouter’s infrastructure to route language-model requests to third-party providers based on pricing, performance and reliability. Previously, Hugging Face used its own routing system, introduced as part of its Inference Providers service in January 2025 , to connect developers with companies running AI models. The service initially launched with four providers: Fal , Replicate , SambaNova and Together AI . The system would select a provider to handle each request, but if that provider encountered a problem, the request failed. With OpenRouter now in the mix, the request can automatically be passed to another provider, meaning that developers should encounter fewer failed requests. Hugging Face co-founder and CEO Clément Delangue sees the partnership as an example of how collaboration between AI companies can make open-weight models more accessible to developers, with each company focusing on its own strengths. “Too many people treat AI as a zero-sum race. Open-source is winning by doing the opposite: collaboration over competition!” “Too many people treat AI as a zero-sum race,” Delangue writes on LinkedIn . “Open-source is winning by doing the opposite: collaboration over competition!” “Hugging Face for storage and collaboration. OpenRouter for inference,” he adds. Stripe, Nvidia and the bigger picture The announcement comes less than a week after Stripe completed its acquisition of OpenRouter , a deal first announced in August and reportedly worth more than $7 billion. Hugging Face, for its part, is also in the process of being acquired by AI chip giant Nvidia for nearly $13 billion. Nvidia, however, is currently grappling with a scandal involving its former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week amid the controversy. At any rate, the OpenRouter integration is already live, initially covering 160 models from 38 AI labs. For Hugging Face, the arrangement means it can offer developers more dependable access to these models without having to maintain its own routing system. In real terms, this means that users can continue chatting directly with AI models on Hugging Face’s model pages, while new interface features let them compare providers by price, speed and uptime, and check performance metrics to help them choose a provider. Hugging Face model page showing the inference interface The integration also works in reverse. OpenRouter users can now send records of their AI model requests to Hugging Face Storage Buckets , where they can examine prompts and responses, build evaluation datasets and prepare models for fine-tuning. Zooming out, OpenRouter gains a direct route into Hugging Face’s enormous developer community, potentially bringing more inference traffic — and revenue –to its new owner, Stripe. Looking ahead, Hugging Face says it plans to let developers connect their OpenRouter accounts directly to Hugging Face, while expanding the integration to cover more AI tasks. It hasn’t provided a timeline for either development. In a blog post announcing the tie-up, OpenRouter’s director of product marketing Sasha Blumenfeld says the partnership builds on the company’s original mission of simplifying access to AI models. “We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond.” “We built OpenRouter so developers can reach many models and providers through one API, use the best model for each task, and count on it to respond,” Blumenfeld writes . “Starting today, that extends to everyone building on Hugging Face.” How OpenRouter chooses providers The integration builds on a…

articles.title: Nvidia board faction angling for Jensen Huang return as CEO, report claims
articles.content: Even though Nvidia says that it does not plan to bring its former CEO Jensen Huang back to the company, that hasn't stopped some of its board members from continuing to lobby for his return. Following the news that some of Huang's allies have formed a "war room" to drive his reinstatement just days after his resignation, one Nvidia employee went so far as to warn that the company faces the possibility of an exodus of "irreplaceable talent" if Huang isn't reinstated. We've even seen U.S. President Trump argue for giving Huang his old job back , but the company said during its November 17 earnings call that wasn't in the cards. Now, Semafor reports that some Nvidia board members aren't taking "no" for an answer. Huang, for his part, has already said that he would be "honored" to return to the company that he resigned from in disgrace just a few days ago . At the time, he admitted to having an affair with a woman who worked for Megaspeed, a controversial Nvidia customer linked to the smuggling of export-controlled AI hardware into China. That woman has also been accused of being a Chinese spy, further complicating an already troublesome matter for Nvidia and Huang. Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer will make an appearance before the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and China Select Committees in early December and are likely to face some difficult questions. But despite all of this, Huang is said to have spoken with at least one Nvidia board member about the possibility of making a return to Nvidia. That meeting took place hours before Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones said on the company’s earnings call that Huang wasn't coming back. The board voted unanimously to accept his resignation, and won't be backtracking. It's reported that three board members don't agree with that stance, while others have already turned their attention to who will replace Huang long-term. Interim CEO Colette Kress is not being considered as a full-time replacement for Huang. Instead, Arm CEO Rene Haas has appeared as a frontrunner for the top job, with the Nvidia board believed to have already made an approach. Marvell CEO Matt Murphy is also another name under consideration, but the ongoing calls for Huang to be brought back into the fold are thought to have put him off. Rene Haas has reportedly been considere It isn't just some of Nvidia's board members who have rallied around Huang. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney have also chimed in , while a Taiwanese skyscraper was used to send messages of support to a man who has proven hugely popular in the country.

articles.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver. How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us? —Amit Katwala Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure. Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power . —Casey Crownhart MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century. As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released. The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple The agency’s classified communications network has gone down. articles.title: Phishing scams get a new watchdog as Moonlock expands to iPhone
articles.content: MacPaw is bringing Moonlock to the iPhone , giving users tools to spot phishing scams and check their security settings without relying on traditional antivirus software. Moonlock on iPhone The iPhone app centers on Scam Detect, which analyzes content that users paste, scan or share with Moonlock. Rather than flagging something as suspicious, it explains what might be wrong, including links that don't match the sender they're supposed to represent. Users can send content to Moonlock directly from other apps through the iOS share sheet. The QR code scanner also lets them inspect a destination before opening it, which could help with scams that hide fraudulent websites behind seemingly ordinary codes. Moonlock's Safe SMS feature takes a more automatic approach. When enabled in iPhone Settings, it filters suspected scam messages from unknown senders into the Junk folder in Messages and explains why each message was flagged. Continue Reading on AppleInsider | Discuss on our Forums

articles.title: Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter
articles.content: For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago . To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set new financial records as demand for its AI accelerators shows no signs of slowing down. The company reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion. 'Momentum is real' "Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," said Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater." For the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The company's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago. (Image credit: Nvidia) As expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the company's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year. (Image credit: Nvidia) One of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The company also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform. (Image credit: Nvidia) "Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress said. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028." Supply commitments reach $390 billion To support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The company's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements. The company expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though…

articles.title: This new scorecard shows whether your favorite retailer is using Flock cameras
articles.content: Automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and other vendors have become increasingly controversial across the country after reports of misuse by officers, high error rates that can lead to dangerous police encounters , and concerns about access by Immigration and Customs Enforcement . Flock, in particular, operates a nationwide camera network, with data from cameras operated in one jurisdiction frequently accessed by investigators from elsewhere, making it hard for local officials to understand and control privacy risks. As a result, while Flock and other providers emphasize that their cameras have been used to investigate legitimate crimes, rescue kidnapped kids, and track stolen cars, many municipalities have ended their contracts, in some cases even covering cameras awaiting removal by the service provider. Many businesses deploy their own automated license plate readers, or ALPRs, to track vehicles in their parking lots, sometimes sharing that information with law enforcement. But since private companies aren’t subject to freedom of information laws, it can be hard to know which businesses have them and what they’re doing with the data they collect. To help people understand in time for the holiday shopping season which stores use the devices, Fight for the Future just released a scorecard listing 10 major retailers and what the organization knows about their use of the cameras. “Retailers also need to be brought into the conversation,” says Reem Suleiman, senior campaign director at Fight for the Future, which previously organized a campaign with home improvement influencers that called on Home Depot and Lowe’s to cut ties with Flock . The chart is based on information the organization received from a questionnaire sent to the retailers and, in cases where they didn’t respond, third-party news reporting, crowdsourced camera spotting, and information from published privacy policies. “We got responses from just a handful of [businesses],” Suleiman says. The exact details vary, and many businesses don’t appear to use the technology at every location. Costco, for instance, told Fight for the Future that it uses ALPR cameras at “less than a dozen locations nationwide,” so it’s difficult to know just from the checklist whether your local branch of a national chain is equipped with the cameras. But it’s easy to see at a glance that many major brands at least acknowledge in their privacy policies that they might be using the technology. Some stores also indicate that they may share information from the devices with law enforcement. The scorecard offers links to retailers’ emails, along with suggested text, to ask them to refrain from using ALPR technology, even if (or perhaps especially if) the details about how they do so may be opaque. Fight for the Future also encourages people to reach out with any tips about retailers that are using the cameras or with requests to add particular stores to the scoresheet. “We don’t have a FOIA request that we can do for companies or a public records act request that we can impose upon companies, but nothing’s stopping us from writing to them,” Suleiman says. “Nothing’s stopping people from letting these companies know what they want and what they expect.”

articles.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
articles.content: In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again. Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whoever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space. About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson . While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago. articles.title: What To Measure When ARR Isn’t Enough
articles.content: By Kenza Zayani In October, reports that OpenAI ‘s annualized revenue was running well below earlier estimates sent AI-linked stocks sharply lower and prompted a fresh round of scrutiny over AI valuations. It also reopened a question investors have been circling for a while: Is ARR still the right way to describe an AI business? The limitations have been understood for some time. ARR was built for software companies selling predictable annual contracts, which is only part of how most AI companies make money. Through the early part of the generative AI boom, growth was steep enough that few people pressed the point. The OpenAI episode has made it harder to leave alone, partly because it showed how much weight public markets now place on a single private company’s numbers. For founders, this is worth paying attention to now rather than later. A cohort of AI companies is reaching the growth-capital stage, and the questions they face in diligence are changing. What ARR was built for Kenza Zayani of RTP Global. ARR became standard in the mid- to late-2000s, when software moved from licence fees to recurring subscriptions. A customer signed for 12 months, revenue became predictable and annualizing it was arithmetic rather than forecasting. The first generation of post-ChatGPT companies inherited it without much examination, despite earning money in a different way. Most now run hybrid models: a subscription base with consumption charges on top, billed against API calls, tokens processed or compute used. A growing number charge per outcome. An annualized figure blends revenue a customer has committed to with revenue that depends on what they use next month. What gets presented as ARR is usually a revenue run rate: recent revenue multiplied out to an annual figure. That is a reasonable way to describe momentum, and a less reliable guide to the year ahead. The first question an investor tends to ask is what the figure actually counts. Companies that sell partly through partners can report either the full value of those sales or only the share they keep, and the two conventions produce very different numbers for the same business. Both are legitimate, but the two are not necessarily comparable. Take two companies both reporting a $10 million annualized run rate. In the first, most of that revenue is contracted, and comes from customers whose usage has expanded steadily over 12 months. In the second, it rests on a handful of customers whose consumption spiked in the last quarter. These are not similar businesses. The first has demonstrated that customers keep coming back and spending more. Nothing in the headline figure tells you that. Looking beyond the headline If a single figure cannot separate those two businesses, the question is what can. The answer depends on the stage. At pre-seed and seed, the number matters. A steep trajectory can point to market demand, to customers willing to pay, and to a team beginning to crack go-to-market. A run rate isn’t generally expected to predict the year at that size. Later you need more. What matters is the revenue behind the number: customer concentration, how much is contracted rather than consumed, how predictable that revenue is, and whether the gross margins hold as volume rises. Retention and expansion are the centerpiece. They tell you how essential a product has become and whether it will still be in use in a few years. Churn is diagnostic in a way a growth figure never is. It can point to demand the product is not answering, pricing that does not match the value, a need that was never really recurring, or a market shallower than it first looked. What investors will expect next ARR has been a staple of how high-growth tech companies demonstrate momentum for such a long time that it’s not likely to disappear anytime soon. What is changing is how much weight that single number can carry on its own. Expect more investors to ask what a figure actually counts, how much…
