articles.title: Sector Snapshot: Investors Turn Up The Volume On Voice AI
articles.content: Voice AI — technology that lets computers understand and generate human speech — is drawing billions of dollars from investors as startups find more ways to put it to work. Companies developing or offering the technology have raised at least $9.5 billion in venture funding so far in 2026, according to Crunchbase data. The recipients range from companies building speech recognition and generation tools to those offering voice agents for customer service. Others use voice AI for creative work or accessibility, or build the infrastructure and chips that power the technology. The broad trend: Investors are putting more money into fewer startups developing or offering voice AI technology and are backing everything from automated customer service to speech generation and content creation. The funding surge also reflects the broader AI boom, with some of the largest rounds going to infrastructure and generative media companies whose businesses extend beyond voice. Multiple companies are raising rounds in quick succession. The numbers: So far in 2026, startups developing or offering voice AI technology have raised $9.5 billion globally, Crunchbase data shows. As of Nov. 11, funding had already exceeded 2025 by 67%, with 154 reported deals versus 273 in 2025. Overall, deal volume is on track to fall for a second consecutive year — pointing to a market where investors are putting more money into fewer companies. Unsurprisingly, given the AI boom, funding for the space has continued to climb in recent years compared to past levels, surging from $2.8 billion in 2021 to $5.7 billion in 2025. Notable rounds The largest rounds in Crunchbase’s voice AI micro-industry went well beyond speech synthesis, encompassing infrastructure, generative media and customer service agents. The biggest individual financing went to Fireworks AI , which raised a $1.5 billion Series D in July at a $17.5 billion valuation. The San Mateo, California-based company is an AI infrastructure provider whose offerings include speech recognition. Atreides Management , Index Ventures and TCV co-led the round, with participation from investors including Nvidia and Lightspeed Venture Partners . San Francisco-based Fal was the largest funding recipient across multiple rounds in 2026, raising $1.65 billion in total. That included a $1.3 billion Series F led by Bessemer Venture Partners , completed in October at a reported $16 billion valuation, doubling its valuation from its $350 million Sequoia Capital -led financing in April. The company provides infrastructure for running image, video and audio models. Customer service AI also attracted substantial investment. San Francisco-based Sierra raised $950 million in May, led by Tiger Global and GV , at a reported $15.8 billion valuation. Its platform lets businesses deploy agents across voice, chat and other customer channels. Meanwhile, Amsterdam-based Wonderful raised a $550 million Series C in September, led by Insight Partners , at a $5 billion valuation. That followed a $150 million Series B in March, bringing its total 2026 funding to $700 million as it expanded from conversational agents into broader enterprise automation. Among companies focused on AI-generated speech, New York-based ElevenLabs announced a $500 million Series D in February, led by Sequoia Capital, at an $11 billion valuation. That was more than triple its valuation a year earlier. Additional institutional and strategic investors joined in later tranches, bringing the Series D total to $561 million. ElevenLabs allows creators, enterprises and others to use AI software to replicate voices in dozens of languages. The company is investing in conversational agents, expressive speech and dubbing. Beijing-based ModelBest , which develops compact AI models that run on devices, also ranks among the largest recipients of funding this year, with a $591 million Series C in July. articles.title: Robots learn human movement patterns to find paths through dense crowds
articles.content: Navigating a bustling train station or airport is a major challenge for people with visual impairments. New research from Örebro University teaches robots to follow the "unwritten rules" of human movement and make their way through dense crowds. In the long term, the technology could serve as a digital complement to guide dogs.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
articles.content: Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort. This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI , a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple. The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers. articles.title: Anthropic’s IPO asks investors to bet that a product can build a company, not the other way around
articles.content: When Anthropic launches its initial public offering this Thursday, it will be another test of how much further the AI industry’s seemingly unchecked growth can go. The company is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion, asking investors to buy into the idea that artificial intelligence will become a major contributor to the economy. But the IPO also asks investors to make a more unusual bet: on a company whose own product could eventually do much of the work of building the business itself. In its amended S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, released last week, Anthropic says that “each new version of a Claude model directly accelerates development of the next.” Claude already helps run experiments, generate training data, and test future models, the company says. As evidence, Anthropic notes that Claude wrote more than 90% of contributions to its code base in September 2026. In the three-month period through September, the daily volume of code contributed per engineer was more than 45 times its 2024 average. Traditionally, companies go public asking investors to bankroll employees who will build and sell better products. Anthropic is pitching something different: a business whose products increasingly help develop their own successors—and, in the process, help build the company itself. There is some precedent for a company using its own technology to improve it. When the software company GitLab went public in 2021, its prospectus described how employees used GitLab’s development platform to identify problems and determine what to build next, a practice known as “dogfooding.” But that was software helping human developers do their jobs, rather than AI increasingly performing the work itself. “It may be the first IPO in which this type of thing is happening,” says Sinan Aral, a professor at MIT Sloan School of Management. Still, Aral cautions against confusing AI’s growing role in developing products with the ability to decide which products should exist in the first place. Claude may be writing code, but humans remain responsible for the more consequential research decisions. “What to do, what goals to have and what to optimize, is generally being decided by human beings,” he says. Even so, experts say Anthropic’s pitch represents a striking departure from the conventional IPO. Until now, discussions of recursive self-improvement—the idea that AI systems could improve their own capabilities—have largely centered on the risks of systems becoming misaligned with human goals, says Jay Ritter, director of the IPO Initiative at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. But Ritter sees a potentially transformative business opportunity, too. Unlike conventional processes of innovation, which often yield diminishing returns, AI-driven self-improvement could theoretically produce exponential gains. That would fundamentally change not only how products are developed, but how the companies behind them operate. “Anthropic and its competitors are companies that are increasingly capable of building themselves,” Ritter says. “Investors are essentially being asked to pay for the electricity to do this.” The prospect also raises questions about how much autonomy Anthropic is willing to grant Claude—and whether a system capable of directing its own development would make decisions aligned with human interests. For now, MIT’s Aral says, the company appears reluctant to surrender that control. Its S-1 contains “a risk section like we’ve never read before,” he says, reflecting the possibility that its technology could eventually begin making consequential decisions on its own. Not everyone is convinced that such a future is imminent, or even plausible. Kirill Skrygan, CEO of JetBrains, a company known for its software development tools, is skeptical that Anthropic has created an AI system capable of improving itself without human intervention. articles.title: Voyager 1 Reaches One Light-Day From Earth
articles.content: NASA's Voyager 1 has become the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth, or 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). This means radio signals will take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft, now nearly 50 years into its mission. "Since light is essentially the maximum speed in the universe (absent using devices like wormholes, or quantum-physics puzzles), it's a big deal -- so big that NASA will be celebrating the milestone by asking fans to shine Morse Code signals at the sky," reports Space.com. From the report: But why will Voyager 2 take nearly a decade longer? It comes down to choices made for speed and science during the twin missions' nearly 50-year journey, specifically during the first bit when they were flying by planets. The result is Voyager 1 is zooming out at a speed of 3.5 Earth-sun distances (astronomical units a year), while Voyager 2 has a more stately speed of 3.1 Earth-sun distances, according to NASA. [...] At any rate, these fast speeds allowed both spacecraft not only to go fast, but to eventually reach interstellar space in 2012 (Voyager 1) and 2018 (Voyager 2), respectively. With the light-day milestone now reached by Voyager 1, it is anticipated the spacecraft could work into the 2030s, as long as their nuclear power sources can last. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, which manages the mission, has been carefully turning off instruments as required, and recently did a "Big Bang" procedure on both spacecraft to redistribute power supplies as best as possible. The idea is to maximize science return on both spacecraft, the only interstellar messengers we have, for as long as possible. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.author: BeauHD

articles.title: A refreshingly practical hidden Gemini treasure
articles.content: A fascinating contrast is shaping up around us here in the land o’ Googley matters, seemingly more with every passing month. On the one side, you’ve got Google, who’s dead-set on pushing Gemini into every place possible and doing everything in its power to convince us to use it — in spite of its alarming little habit of, y’know, getting stuff wrong . More often than not, the company (like most tech players these days) is also focused on impractical processes and overly complex use cases that few actual humans have any interest in embracing. On the other side sits us — the (allegedly) human mammal-people who are toting around all this technology, often begrudgingly, and mostly just looking for simple ways to make it more useful and simultaneously less intrusive in our lives . With exceedingly rare exception, nearly everyone I’ve chatted with in 2026 shares the same basic sentiment — that AI feels invasive and annoying, that most of what it’s offering has nothing to do with our current wants and needs, and that the type of tech we actually want somehow keeps getting worse as a result of its intrusion. We need look no further than the Google Assistant-Gemini contrast on Android or the frustrating devolution of so-called smart speakers and screens for some all-too-relatable examples. That’s why I, like so many of you, mostly roll my eyes at every new AI announcement and its lack of any real impact on my day-to-day life. And that’s also why I’m constantly on the prowl for ways Gemini can actually be useful when it comes to real-world productivity. Perhaps not surprisingly, the discoveries that resonate the most tend to be the simplest, least flashy features imaginable — and that’s absolutely the case with the genuinely useful Gemini gem I want to share with you today. [Get fresh tips in your inbox with my free Android Intelligence newsletter — something new and useful from me to ye every single Friday!] Gemini’s quiet contact creating capability Seriously — this is so simple, it’s almost silly. It isn’t an effective illustration of the sheer processing power of the latest Gemini 7.23b Bouillabaisse model (which I’m fairly certain was the subject of a recent announcement somewhere). But, unlike most of that malarkey, it’s actually something you’ll use and that’ll make your life easier. (Imagine that!) It’s a quick ‘n’ easy way to import anyone’s information into a properly formatted, ready-to-roll contact on your phone with approximately seven seconds of active effort. And it works in two equally useful ways: First, the next time you encounter an actual printed business card out and about on your adventures, fire up Gemini, tap the plus icon within its prompt box and select “Camera,” and snap a fast photo of the card — then just tell Gemini to save that as a new contact. The very first time you do it, you’ll have to grant Gemini access to your contacts and all of that. But once that’s out of the way, the system will simply scan the info, put all the details into all the right places, and confirm that you want to save it. A fast photo and confirmation, and our complete new contact is created. JR Raphael, Foundry A quick confirmation later, and boom: That person is officially in your contacts , without the need for any third-party importing apps or time-wasting manual entry. Every last detail visible on the card is present in the right place in the Contacts app. JR Raphael, Foundry Second, this same feat will work with any virtual contact info you encounter anywhere on your device — in an email, on a website, you name it. Whenever you’re looking at someone’s info on your screen, just fire up Gemini and ask it to save the info you’re seeing as a contact. It’ll handle it in the exact same way. Whether the info is on a physical card or on your screen somewhere, the contact-creating process is essentially the same. JR Raphael, Foundry It may not be the kind of thing that’ll make it into the next big Google keynote or Gemini announcement,…

articles.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
articles.content: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary. Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and…

articles.title: Jeff Bezos’s $41 billion AI startup Prometheus is shrouded in secrecy. We found out who’s building it
articles.content: For many in the tech industry, physical AI is the next world to conquer. While developers of large language models like OpenAI and Anthropic seek to push reasoning models distilled on billions of streams of text to their limits, an emerging crop of companies are focusing on an even more ambitious goal: developing AI programs designed to speak the language of physics . Should they succeed, these firms have a stake in everything from building models that might power self-driving manufacturing or enable drug discovery to those that can take on plane design and weapons development. The promise is enormous. Whoever cracks physical AI could control a slice of the software stack that becomes critical to a host of industries—and worth many, many billions. Already, a growing list of companies are racing to stake their claim. Among the buzziest is Prometheus , a startup backed by Jeff Bezos that’s already flush with cash. Bezos isn’t just bankrolling Prometheus. He’s also coleading the company, marking his first executive role since stepping down as Amazon’s CEO in 2021. His cofounder is Vik Bajaj, a Stanford professor who previously led science operations at Verily, Alphabet’s health technology venture. Prometheus was incubated in 2024 at Foresite Labs, which Bajaj led, with support from the venture capital firm Arch Venture Partners. A number of Prometheus employees also appear to have come from firms associated with Bajaj. By combing through LinkedIn and researchers’ personal websites, Fast Company identified 130 people who say they’re currently working for Prometheus, and assembled what appears to be the first public database of its kind. Prometheus employs approximately 250 people, including numerous accomplished AI researchers, some of whose names have not been publicly disclosed. The company is recruiting not only AI model developers but also experts in fields like aerospace and chemistry, a strong hint that it may one day target manufacturing and healthcare customers. Employees bring expertise in ocean engineering, energy engineering, mathematics, and even high-performance computing. In this Subscriber Exclusive, you’ll discover: An exclusive database of the more than 130 people who have publicly joined Prometheus, Bezos’s buzzy and secretive AI startup What those employees’ expertise tells us about where the company is headed, and direct insights from people within Prometheus about what they’re actually building A list of rival companies competing in the physical AI space—and their investors Deep insight into what physical AI actually is, and why the market could be worth hundreds of billions Why Bezos’s other, more renowned companies, Amazon and Blue Origin, stand to benefit most if Prometheus succeeds At a Semafor event on November 17, Bezos and Bajaj said they’ve spent much of their funding on compute and have built one single multi-physics model. Thus far, Prometheus has built a neural surrogate for numerical simulation and has used the technology to design a range of hardware, including an experiment that involved having the company’s models redesign the Mars helicopter. This next AI revolution needs AI tools trained not on text but on data from the physical world, as well as subject-matter experts who can ensure that models are distilling a common core of engineering principles that can extend across myriad domains. This, in turn, involves recruiting not just AI coders but plenty of people with expertise in the physical realm, whether that’s manufacturing automotive parts or running biology labs. “Most fundamentally, the biggest challenge is just the sheer breadth of what we’re doing. Engineering is vast. There’s no such thing as an engineer,” one leading AI expert and early-stage Prometheus employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, tells Fast Company . “This idea of building something that’s general enough to cover all of that space, that’s…

articles.title: The smartest AI might be the one that leaves us alone
articles.content: One of the ideas I’m always trying to tell my students is that their brains are something, an asset, if you like, they need to protect. The human brain is an amazing optimizer: Provide it with an effortless way to achieve something, and it will quickly start to use it. We used to memorize a ton of phone numbers a few decades ago. Now we can hardly memorize our own, simply because our brain knows the number is a few clicks away. A clear example is why I never use AI to write my articles: simply because, for me, in my personal methodology as a professor of innovation, writing is my way of making concepts stick in my brain, concepts I will need later to teach and discuss. If I ask ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, or any other chatbot to write my articles for me, I would lose much of the learning that writing gives me. This doesn’t mean I don’t use AI: I can use it to translate certain parts, to search for relevant articles to back up an assertion, or to assess whether the concepts I try to explain come across clearly. But I don’t want to use it for writing, because writing is a skill I want to protect. And like a muscle, if you don’t exercise it, it quickly atrophies. For a manager, the skill worth protecting might be decision-making: An AI that makes every choice could undermine precisely the judgment that person needs to develop. The useful behavior depends on the objective, and sometimes that objective requires the system to hold back. What happens when we move from personal to corporate use? Can an AI learn when its intervention would make things worse? That capability might receive very little applause in a product demonstration, but it could be enormously valuable in practice. The sales agent that lets us be Imagine a company using a sales agent. When it identifies a customer approaching renewal, it follows a standard procedure: It quickly reviews the account, writes a personalized email, offers a discount, and schedules a follow-up. All of it in mere seconds. And the audience claps enthusiastically. But what if our customer would have renewed anyway? Then, the end result is that we have wasted an interaction, risked alienating the customer, and surrendered margin unnecessarily. What if our customer is a happy one, and the right thing to do would have been just to wait for him or her to renew voluntarily? Even when all tasks are perfectly executed, the decision to perform them could have been perfectly wrong. The cost of being helpful We know how this feels when we’re working with real people: Experienced employees often develop a sense of when to follow up, when to escalate an issue, and when making too many interventions will look messy, send the wrong signal, or make the customer upset. How do they know that? It comes with experience; it’s learning that compounds over time, with more and more iterations. That judgment is something we pay to have. However, when we evaluate AI, we tend to be fascinated with visible activity—with messages generated, tasks completed, workflows executed, etc. The equivalent is if we were dealing with a hyperactive employee. And as we probably know, someone who sends twice the number of messages is probably not twice as valuable. In other words, just because an action can be automated and, therefore, performed easily, doesn’t mean that we should be performing it all the time. Look what happens with AI coding assistants: In “ When to show a suggestion? articles.title: Apple is turning your iPhone into a car key for 3 popular brands. Unlocking is only the beginning
articles.content: Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC drivers will now be able to unlock their vehicles with their phones. As first reported by MacRumors , General Motors announced that it has begun rolling out the Apple Wallet feature to select models. More vehicles are expected to be added over time. Eligible customers will receive notifications in the “What’s New” section of their vehicle’s app when digital-key support is available. Users will be able to use their smartphones or Apple Watches much like a physical key to unlock their vehicles. GM said supported vehicles will automatically unlock as a driver approaches and lock as the driver walks away. According to the company, the vehicle’s trunk and climate control system will be accessible with the new Apple Wallet feature. “The digital key experience will continue to evolve beyond simply unlocking and starting a vehicle. By leveraging ultra-wideband technology, GM is laying the groundwork for more deeply integrated and personalized experiences like automatically adjusting vehicle settings as drivers approach and other intelligent features that make ownership more convenient,” said the company in a press release . Apple first announced the concept at its Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2020. It later launched exclusively for select 2021 BMW 5 Series models. Since then, the tech company has added other major automakers, such as Mercedes-Benz, Hyundai, Kia, Genesis, and Audi, to the offering. The digital key may work even when a phone’s battery is dead. The company said that depending on a user’s iPhone model, keys could still be available even when a device needs to be charged . However, it warned that they will be available only for up to five hours. The evolution of digital keys Samsung rolled out its own version of the digital keys in 2021. In October, Samsung announced it would support digital keys for select GM vehicles. The digital key is the latest evolution in car-key technology. In the 1980s, automakers began using radio frequencies to create remote keyless entry fobs. In 2008, Nissan and tech company Sharp launched a mobile phone with a built-in intelligent car-key chip in Japan. Then, in 2017, Tesla advanced the concept by making its smartphone app the primary, default key for the Model 3, replacing the standard physical key fob. Apple and GM did not immediately respond to requests for comment. articles.title: SID AI Releases SID-2 Agentic Search Model With 0.720 NDCG Swarm Mode
articles.content: SID AI has released SID-2 , its second-generation agentic search model, alongside SID-2 Swarm. SID-2 is an agentic search model from SID AI that searches your data, reads results and returns ranked document IDs. It replaces fixed RAG pipelines with a model that decides what to search next. TL;DR Size: Context window is 262k tokens per the report (256k on sid.ai/models ). Runs on: Hosted API at platform.sid.ai , plus Baseten and SageMaker reference paths. SID’s latency figures assume 1 B200 GPU at 8 concurrent queries. Performance: A single agent matches Claude Opus 5.5 on retrieval quality. Swarms beat every model SID tested. Best: SID-2 Swarm (12 agents) scores 0.720 NDCG , above GPT-6 Astra at 0.704. Worst: SID-2 Low scores 0.556 NDCG , 0.148 below GPT-6 Astra. Astra still leads on California law, SEC filings and FiQA. Bottom line: Best: frontier-level retrieval at a fraction of the latency. Worst: no disclosed size, weights or independent evals yet. What is SID-2 and how does it work? SID-2 is a small search specialist, not a general chat model. A static pipeline runs rewrite, embed, search and rerank in a fixed order. SID-2 instead searches, reads results, adapts and searches again . Developers implement the search tools against their own backend. A text_search tool covers keyword search and a search tool covers vector search. The model ends each episode by calling report_helpful_ids with a ranked list. No reindexing or data movement is required , since SID-2 only sees what your tools return. SID-2 Swarm runs several agents that message each other and fork their context into new agents. Each agent explores a separate slice of the corpus. SID argues search gains more from reading more documents than from reasoning harder about each one. What are reasoning effort and Metric Steering? SID-2 offers low, medium and high reasoning effort. Each level was trained as a separate expert, then merged with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Metric Steering lets users target NDCG, F1 or Recall@k, with k from 1 to 50. On SID’s 506-question validation set, SID-2 at high effort scores 0.14 to 0.22 higher per metric than the base model. How was SID-2 trained? Training used 2-stage reinforcement learning. Stage 1 optimizes retrieval quality only. Stage 2 adds a multiplicative latency penalty that applies only to positive rewards. A proposer-solver self-play loop generated hard queries against a frozen SID-1 solver. SID reports a 6x training-throughput gain over SLIME’s default setup. How does SID-2 perform on benchmarks? SID built a 506-question benchmark across 19 corpora. These include HotpotQA, Enron emails, SEC filings, PubMed and BrowseComp-Plus. All numbers below are self-reported from Tables 2 to 4 of the report . SID-2 Medium: 0.585 NDCG in 3.11 s, versus Claude Opus 5.5 (medium) at 0.577 in 25.1 s. SID-2 Swarm, 6 agents: 0.701 NDCG in 17.7 s, versus GPT-6 Astra (max) at 0.704 in 135 s. SID-2 Swarm, 12 agents: 0.720 NDCG, the highest score in the table. Baselines: BM25 scores 0.260 and vector search plus reranker scores 0.287. Swarm leads on 11 of 19 corpora. On WixQA, a single high-effort agent matches Astra at about 232x lower cost. At its lowest effort, SID-2 beats 4 parallel SID-1 runs with 13x fewer FLOPs. articles.title: Battery startup Sila lands potential $1B Panasonic deal, plans Central Wash. expansion adding 500 jobs
articles.content: Sila’s Moses Lake facility will be expanded to meet demand from Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America and other customers. (Sila Photo) Sila , a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company plans to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years. Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance. Sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used. The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO. “This is a really important blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he said. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.” Related Sila’s Gene Berdichevsky on the future of battery manufacturing While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components. Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers. Berdichevsky said Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller. In August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized. The startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington. The company has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round announced in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook. Seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea. Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced plans for a factory in Spain. Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky said. “This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he said. The first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. articles.title: Hacker Pleads Guilty to Leak of Grand Theft Auto VI Footage
articles.content: Artion Kurtaj, the British hacker responsible for leaking early footage of Grand Theft Auto VI in 2022, pleaded guilty Monday to six offenses stemming from cyberattacks against Rockstar Games, Uber and Revolut. The 21-year-old, who was previously deemed unfit to stand trial due to severe autism, carried out the hacking spree "using a mobile phone and an Amazon Fire Stick connected to a hotel room television," reports The Record, "despite bail restrictions limiting his access to the internet." From the report: Now 21, he admitted six offenses at Woolwich Crown Court on Monday, four under the Computer Misuse Act, one of fraud and one of possession of a mobile phone in prison, and is due to be sentenced next week. Kurtaj "used sophisticated hacking techniques to carry out a sustained campaign of cyberattacks, causing serious disruption to major international business and putting sensitive information at risk," said specialist prosecutor Robert Hutchinson. "The defendant was involved in a hacking group responsible for attacks which caused millions of dollars in losses. His offending was calculated and, even after being charged with serious offenses, he continued to target organizations, demonstrating a persistent disregard for the harm he was causing and the law. This was an exceptionally complex and challenging case, but despite his efforts to conceal his identity online, our specialist prosecutors were able to work closely with the City of London Police and international law enforcement partners to build a strong case that exposed his actions and resulted in his guilty pleas," said Hutchinson. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Anthropic Adds Code Mode to Claude Code: Claude Now Chains Tool Calls in JavaScript
articles.content:
Anthropic has added Code Mode to Claude Code as an experimental, opt-in feature. Claude Code Code Mode is a mode in which Claude writes JavaScript that makes several tool calls in 1 step. It shipped in Claude Code v2.1.323 last week . For developers, it changes how the agent spends round-trips on multi-step work. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Works with: It works with Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.2. Runs on: An interactive terminal session on the native build, v2.1.323 or later. Windows needs Git for Windows. Anthropic API or Claude subscription only. Performance: Anthropic publishes no benchmark or token-saving figure for Code Mode. Best: Background code can run for up to 2 hours while you keep talking to Claude. Worst: Code that Claude waits on stops after 10 minutes. No Bedrock, Google Cloud, Foundry, -p , Agent SDK, VS Code or Desktop. Bottom line: Best: related tool calls run as 1 program. Worst: narrow availability and coarser auto-mode review. What is Code Mode in Claude Code? Without Code Mode, Claude requests each Bash, Read or Edit call directly. It reads every result before choosing the next step. With Code Mode, Claude writes a piece of JavaScript, and Claude Code runs it in your session. According to the docs , one piece of code can run commands in parallel. It can feed one result into the next call. It can also return only the output Claude needs to read. Anthropic’s example raises a retry limit. The code finds the file, edits it and runs the tests: Copy Code Copied Use a different Browser const files = await $`rg -l "function retryPolicy" src`.text(); const target = files.trim().split("\n")[0]; await edit(target, "maxAttempts: 3", "maxAttempts: 5"); ({ edited: target, tests: $`npm test -- retryPolicy`.nothrow() }); In the conversation, you see the tool calls, such as the diff. You do not see the code by default. Press Ctrl+O to open the transcript viewer and expand a collapsed Code row. Play side by side Blue dashed = model turn. Clay = tool work. 
const files = await $`rg -l "function retryPolicy" src`.text(); const target = files.trim().split("\n")[0]; await edit(target, "maxAttempts: 3", "maxAttempts: 5"); ({ edited: target, tests: $`npm test -- retryPolicy`.nothrow() });

You see the tool calls (such as the diff), not the code. Press Ctrl+O to open the transcript and expand a Code row.

Set the variable
macOS / Linux / WSLPowerShellsettings.json 
CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 claude
$env:CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE = "1" claude
// ~/.claude/settings.json { "env": { "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE": "1" } }
Steps
  1. Run claude --version; update if older than v2.1.323
  2. Start with the variable set to 1
  3. Pick "Yes, turn on Code Mode"
  4. Give Claude a many-tool-call task
  5. Press Ctrl+O to read the code
A 0 in your shell or settings wins over a 1. Admins can set 0 in managed settings to block it org-wide, but cannot force it on.

articles.title: Helping AI text detectors keep up with changing conditions
articles.content: A teacher who believes a student’s term paper may have been written by a large language model (LLM) can use a tool for detecting artificial intelligence-generated text to help confirm their suspicions. But the teacher may want to think twice before putting all their trust in the detector. Researchers from MIT and Cornell University showed that such detection tools, which are AI models themselves, can be fooled by AI-generated text disguised to appear as if it were written by a human. Detectors can also fail to identify AI text due to natural shifts in writing habits over time or the emergence of new LLMs. In a new paper , the researchers demonstrated how a special training technique makes an AI detector more accurate and resilient to deception, even as human and AI writing constantly changes. They employed a method called test-time adaptation, which allows a deployed detection model to learn from new, unlabeled data by adjusting its inner workings on the fly. In this way, the model adapts to unseen inputs without being retrained from scratch. In experiments, a commercial detector could only identify about 27 percent of AI-generated text that had been disguised, while the new approach achieved 93 percent accuracy. This method could help educators, editors, publishers, and hiring managers flag LLM-generated writing that people try to pass off as human-written. It could also be used by cybersecurity experts to prevent email phishing scams or identify search engine optimization fraud. “There are many high-stakes contexts where people really care about the identity of the author, from scientific publishing to short story competitions. We’ve shown that test-time adaptation allows your AI detector to be much more robust, even with continual adversarial behavior by AI users,” says study co-author Manish Raghavan, the Drew Houston (2005) Career Development Professor at the MIT Sloan School of Management, who also holds an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), and is a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). He is joined on the paper by lead author Kevin Ren, graduate student at Cornell Tech, and senior author Nikhil Garg, an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. The research will be presented at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems. Duping the detectors The proliferation of LLMs that generate human-like text has led to a plethora of commercial AI-detection tools to help people identify whether a piece of writing was authored by a human. But these detection tools can fail when the text they evaluate significantly differs from the text they were taught to identify. This is known as a distribution shift. Detector developers typically train their models by gathering text from the internet that they know to be either AI- or human-generated. They train the model to tell the difference. However, once the detector is released, people might change the way they write or the way they use AI to generate text. For instance, a human in 2030 may write about different topics using new analogies that weren’t common for someone writing in 2010. A detector trained with 2010 data might be unfamiliar with this new writing style and incorrectly mark human-written text as AI-generated. The release of a detection model also creates a cat-and-mouse game between its developers and users who want to bypass it. These individuals can run AI-generated text through an automated “humanizer” software tool that modifies it to appear human-written to the detector. “After the company releases a model, a bunch of ‘humanizers’ pop up to try to beat it, so the company tries to incorporate this humanized text into their training so the detector can identify it, and so on. It’s like rinse-and-repeat. The cycle can go on forever,” says Ren. The researchers explored whether test-time adaptation (TTA) can make an AI detector…

articles.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. Erica Schwartz, director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has previously said losing elimination status won't lead to changes in the federal response. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities," Schwartz said on Tuesday. "Losing a designation doesn't mean we abandon an evidence-based approach. It means we remain focused on stopping outbreaks." Read more of this story at Slashdot.

articles.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
articles.content: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC , CNN , Equifax , Ledger and Zoom , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content. The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge. According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s. Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “ DarkSword ” and “ Coruna ,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote . “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.” “We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.” Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content. One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing. “So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to…
